title: Tracking Space Weather with 3D Printed Fluxgate Magnetometer Sensors
lead_organization: Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) — Greenbelt, Maryland
description: We propose developing a breakthrough capability to 3D print miniaturized single-axis fluxgate magnetometers within ceramic structures, enabling large-scale, consistent manufacturing of science-grade sensors for space weather monitoring. This innovation addresses current production bottlenecks in GSFC's Miniaturized Science Magnetometer (MSM) by replacing labor-intensive hand assembly with streamlined additive manufacturing. Partnering with Marshall Space Flight Center, we will print ceramic structures with embedded metal coils, ensuring precision and reproducibility of four key design features: (1) wire thickness, (2) turn spacing, (3) number of turns, and (4) rigid structure maintaining mechanical and electrical stability. The hollow core (~300 µm diameter) allows the sensitive magnetic core to be loaded as a final step, minimizing contact that can damage magnetic domains.
benefits: 3D-printed miniaturized single-axis fluxgate magnetometers in ceramic structures; large-scale, consistent manufacturing of science-grade sensors; addresses GSFC MSM production bottlenecks; precise and reproducible control of four key design features (wire thickness, turn spacing, turns, rigid structure).

title: Automated Sampling of Microphysiological Systems for in situ Bioanalysis
lead_organization: Ames Research Center (ARC) — Moffett Field, California
description: To study the effects of deep space stressors on organ and tissue systems, flight instrumentation consisting of autonomous microphsiological systems hardware with bioanalysis capability is attractive. Our objective is to deliver an integrated flight-compatible and autonomous MPS fluidic instrumentation and flight-compatible and autonomous magnetic electrochemical enzyme linked immunosorbent assay (Mag-EC ELISA). The coupling of these technologies will enable in situ studies of the effects of stressors associated with long term space habitation.
benefits: To study the effects of deep space stressors on organ and tissue systems during flight and without human or animal subjects, autonomous MPS with in situ bioanalysis is required. This project will accelerate the development of MPS hardware towards flight, enabling the study of deep space stressors on organ and tissue systems.

title: Modeling Piezoelectric Materials for Active Dust Mitigation
lead_organization: Ames Research Center (ARC) — Moffett Field, California
description: During space exploration missions on lunar or Mars surfaces, improved dust mitigation technologies are in urgent need to protect the crews and equipment. Currently, electrodynamic dust shielding (EDS) is most widely used. The self-sensing transparent piezoelectric surface acoustic wave (TP-SAW) active dust mitigator has been proved to be orders of magnitude higher in energy efficiency than EDS, and it can remove both charged and uncharged particles while EDS can only repel the charged ones. The performance of TP-SAW depends on the piezoelectric coefficient d. Piezoelectric materials such as LiNbO3 can properly function at a very wide range of temperatures (T) from cryogenic to elevated, but their piezoelectric coefficients are small. Relaxor ferroelectric solid solutions such as PMN-PT and PZN-PT, have very large piezoelectric coefficients at room temperature, but these ceramics cannot be used cryogenically. We propose to computationally search/design piezoelectric materials which would have piezoelectric coefficients similar to those of PMN-PT and PZN-PT and which can be used reliably at lunar surface temperature range. We will compute d vs T using the methods developed/tailored for shape memory alloys. The candidate materials will be synthesized and characterized by our experimental collaborators in LaRC.
benefits: We propose to computationally search/design piezoelectric materials which would have piezoelectric coefficients similar to those of PMN-PT and PZN-PT and which can be used reliably at lunar surface temperature range. We will compute d vs T using the methods developed/tailored for shape memory alloys. The candidate materials will be synthesized and characterized by our experimental collaborators in LaRC.

title: Generative AI Rescheduling Assistant for Autonomous Deconfliction of Crew-Spacecraft Timelines
lead_organization: Ames Research Center (ARC) — Moffett Field, California
description: This proposal addresses this challenge through a ground test campaign designed to evaluate the sensitivity of flight-state reconstruction to measured inputs and instrumentation configurations across a dynamic mid-flight event. The campaign will consist of dropping 8-12 instrumented entry capsules from approximately 60 m, each employing different sensor suites and data acquisition architectures. Reconstructed trajectories will be compared against ground-truth observations, with emphasis on reconstruction performance through the ejection event. The Stratospheric Projectile Experiment of Entry Dynamics (SPEED) platform, a novel test architecture under development at NASA Ames, provides the experimental framework for this investigation. Leveraging a gantry-based SPEED drop test, the proposed campaign will inform refinement of measurement integration strategies, avionics configurations, and data processing approaches, supporting future free-flight dynamic stability testing.
benefits: Playbook is a NASA Ames flagship software, built by the investment of multiple missions and research projects. While Playbook is used in NASA analogs (like CHAPEA) and spaceflight robotic missions (like CLPS & Mars2020), it has not been selected for initial Artemis missions because Playbook has not had the opportunity to demonstrate greater efficiencies over existing platforms. Evidence for improved efficiencies at low cost (using existing, available AI tools) is an essential acceptance component for future Artemis and Mars missions. This small investment by Ames would allow our team to make a stronger proposal for Playbook as the next generation planning and scheduling platform for M2M.

title: Sensitivity Analysis of Flight-State Reconstruction Across a Dynamic Mid-Flight Event
lead_organization: Ames Research Center (ARC) — Moffett Field, California
description: Accurate reconstruction of entry vehicle flight state from onboard measurements is critical to free-flight testing of dynamic stability, particularly when measurements must be integrated across rapid mid-flight events. Discrete separation or ejection events introduce abrupt changes in vehicle dynamics and measurement conditions, increasing sensitivity to sensor configuration, timing, and data integration assumptions. Understanding these sensitivities is essential for ensuring reliable post-flight trajectory reconstruction.
benefits: The proposed ground test campaign provides critical validation of flight-state reconstruction capability, increasing the technical maturity and credibility of the SPEED test architecture. This validation positions SPEED as a data-rich capability for future NASA missions requiring aerodynamic performance and dynamic stability assessment, enabling risk reduction prior to flight. By strengthening confidence in post-flight reconstruction, this work enhances NASA Ames’ ability to compete for externally funded mission support, technology maturation efforts, and strategic partnerships. The results also increase the attractiveness of SPEED to commercial partners seeking cost-effective preflight risk reduction, supporting reimbursable testing, partnerships, and potential licensing through the Tech Transfer program. Overall, this investment improves the readiness, utility, and marketability of a unique Ames-developed test capability.

title: Magnetic-nozzle Arcjet eXperiments for Wall-loading, Erosion, and Lifetime Limits (MAXWELL)
lead_organization: Ames Research Center (ARC) — Moffett Field, California
description: AIVFC targets rising operations costs for productive but aging missions (e.g., IRIS) that depend on legacy ground systems with low autonomy—driving high staffing, time-consuming alert handling, and training burden. By introducing an LLM-enabled “virtual flight controller,” AIVFC reduces operator workload, accelerates anomaly response, and lowers overall mission operations cost. The architecture is modular and extensible, enabling reuse across other legacy missions with similar infrastructure (e.g., BioSentinel), scaling savings without ground-up redevelopment.
benefits: The return on investment for this IRAD is realized through enhanced capability, reduced operational downtime, and improved utilization of existing NASA assets. Evaluating a non-contact nozzle addresses erosion-driven operational limits, repeatability degradation, and rigidity associated with fixed hardware configurations. The resulting improvements (higher-quality datasets, more adaptable test campaigns, and increased confidence in data used for material qualification and model validation) provide durable value independent of scalable deployment.

title: Artificial Intelligence Virtual Flight Controller (AIVFC)
lead_organization: Ames Research Center (ARC) — Moffett Field, California
description: We propose to leverage the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph (IRIS) extended mission as a testbed to develop an AI Virtual Flight Controller (AIVFC) tool for anomaly resolution. The ground-based AIVFC will analyze IRIS spacecraft core systems telemetry, provide real-time recommendations to human controllers, and advance the TRL of AI-based Fault Detection, Isolation, and Recovery (FDIR) methods. No direct commanding to the spacecraft will be performed by AI in this initial effort. The AIVFC framework will be made available to other missions and will serve as a surrogate model to infuse the design of future AI autonomy tools for Earth Independent Operations (EIO) under the Mars Campaign Office (MCO). The AIVFC tool will use 12+ years of IRIS core systems telemetry and simulation data to train AI models for anomaly detection, prediction, and resolution. The tool will be deployed in the IRIS Mission Operations environment as a ground-based decision support system that monitors real-time telemetry, alerts operators to anomalies, and recommends corrective actions. Flight controllers will validate tool performance during real-time operations, enabling rapid Technology Readiness Level (TRL) advancement from laboratory demonstrations to operational validation (TRL 6) within 2 years. This activity establishes an AI operations framework to enable cost-effective reuse of AI methods across missions. The project directly addresses the need for increased autonomy in future exploration missions where Earth-based intervention is limited, such as the Mars Campaign Office Earth Independent Operations (MCO EIO). By demonstrating AI-enabled anomaly resolution in IRIS extended operations, this effort will reduce labor costs, improve operational resilience, and build confidence in AI adoption for NASA flight projects.
benefits: This activity establishes an AI operations framework to enable cost-effective reuse of AI methods across missions. The project directly addresses the need for increased autonomy in future exploration missions where Earth-based intervention is limited, such as the Mars Campaign Office Earth Independent Operations (MCO EIO). By demonstrating AI-enabled anomaly resolution in IRIS extended operations, this effort will reduce labor costs, improve operational resilience, and build confidence in AI adoption for NASA flight projects.

title: Multiple Reflection Time-of-Flight Mass Spectrometer
lead_organization: Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) — Greenbelt, Maryland
description: We propose to advance early development of miniature, high resolution Multiple Reflection Time-of-Flight (MRTOF) mass spectrometers with the potential to deliver science measurement capabilities far beyond the current state of the art, positioning GSFC to lead multiple science and exploration missions (Mars, Ocean Worlds, Moon, Outer Planets). The MRTOF offers three transformational features: (1) mass resolution (m/Dm) exceeding 10^5 FWHM to distinguish near-isobars; (2) miniaturization to 25 cm length and 5-7 kg total mass, smaller and lighter than any competing instrument; and (3) coupling to advanced GSFC-unique ionization and ion optical front-end technologies. Together these constitute a new measurement architecture of broad applicability across multiple mission classes and domains.
benefits: Mass resolution >10^5 FWHM; miniaturization to 25 cm/5–7 kg; coupling to GSFC-unique ionization and ion optical front-end technologies; transformational measurement architecture applicable across Mars, Ocean Worlds, Moon, and Outer Planets missions.

title: FUN4D: A New Paradigm for Time-Dependent Simulations
lead_organization: Langley Research Center (LaRC) — Hampton, Virginia
description: Conventional CFD time advancement is inherently serial, one step at a time, creating a scalability barrier. This barrier limits the ability of long‑duration unsteady simulations to fully utilize modern exascale systems. The FUN4D project aims to develop an unsteady-flow solver that exploits temporal concurrency and space-time grid adaptation, breaking through the scalability limits of traditional time-marching approaches and enabling scalable, efficient, high-fidelity, long-duration aerodynamic simulations
benefits: This project aims to develop an unsteady-flow solver that exploits temporal concurrency and space-time grid adaptation, breaking through the scalability limits of traditional time-marching approaches and enabling scalable, efficient, high-fidelity, long-duration aerodynamic simulations. Specific target outcomes include: Generate 4D unstructured simplicial space-time grids. Develop FUN4D, a space‑time unstructured-grid solver for high-fidelity unsteady flow simulations. Demonstrate superior scalability, accuracy and efficiency relative to traditional time-marching methods for representative aerodynamic configurations.

title: Surviving Lunar Night with Solid State Battery Systems
lead_organization: Langley Research Center (LaRC) — Hampton, Virginia
description: Conventional lithium ion batteries using liquid electrolytes would freeze under ultralow temperatures. A solid-state battery system with sustainable sodium-based solid electrolyte that never freezes is proposed to survive and operate through ultracold lunar night to significantly improve the reliability of energy storage systems for lunar surface and extreme space environment operations.
benefits: Safe, resilient, and low-cost SSB system for extreme space environment. Building on success from Year 1 in high conductivity Na solid electrolytes, start further investigating Na SSB full cell architectures tailored toward low temperature operation. Fabricate Na SSB cells and test material performance in wide temperature settings. Test extreme temperature survivability (-170°C - +120°C) and operation (-40°C - +100°C) of Na SSB cells under thermal vacuum conditions.

title: TrajGPT: Beyond Low Earth Orbit Trajectory Generation via Machine Learning
lead_organization: Johnson Space Center (JSC) — Houston, Texas
description: Ensuring a deep space crew can arrive at their destination at the appropriate time and return safely requires detailed planning. Current design methods involve generating millions of trajectories and analyzing countless permutations of variables such as launch date and time, propellant budgets, and abort options. This is too complex to be done onboard in real-time; however, changing the modeling techniques may enable onboard capabilities that could improve crew autonomy and operational flexibility. In year one, the TrajGPT IRAD project investigated use of Machine Learning (ML) to possibly replace the current brute-force methods of physics models. The results to date have shown promise and warrant further investigation. In year two, the model will be trained on additional scenarios and results will be validated against current ground software. Year two objectives include demonstrating generation of 1) no-fail ascent trajectories every 1 minute through a launch window and 2) on-orbit abort trajectories at various points in a lunar mission.
benefits: The general capability could be broadly applicable to both crewed and uncrewed missions involving spaceflight. ​For crewed missions, a change in modeling techniques may enable onboard capabilities that could improve crew autonomy and operational flexibility, vital to the success of future Mars missions.

title: The design of fibrous insulation to minimize radiative heat transfer for TPS
lead_organization: Langley Research Center (LaRC) — Hampton, Virginia
description: Opacifiers are known to improve mitigation of radiative heat transfer in fibrous insulations. The analysis will be extended to 2-D space, fibrous mediums with short fibers and opacifiers will be added, and thermal testing of Opacified Fibrous Insulation (OFI) will be completed. The analysis capability will be validated by measured optical properties and thermal performance of Q-fiber Felt and OFI.
benefits: Predictive capability enables optimal TPS design and manufacturing, including opacified fibrous insulation (OFI). Develop a physics-based capability to predict radiative heat transfer in fibrous insulation. Study Q-Fiber Felt and OFI by SEM, optical, and thermal vacuum testing and validate the analysis with experiment.

title: Full-Scale Trash-to-Gas System Demonstration
lead_organization: Kennedy Space Center (KSC) — Kennedy Space Center, Florida
description: Manufacture, build, and test a full-scale, Trash-to-Gas system for a ground demonstration. Infuse lessons learned from prior successful sub-scale demonstrations of the technology in microgravity via suborbital flight testing.
benefits: Full-scale prototype system demonstrated in the ground environment for relevant durations (~33 days).

title: Orbital Drag Calibration Object Design Study
lead_organization: Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) — Greenbelt, Maryland
description: Every satellite in Low Earth Orbit (LEO) is continuously perturbed by atmospheric drag — a force that, if poorly characterized, leads to inaccurate orbit predictions, unnecessary collision avoidance maneuvers, uncertainty in reentry forecasts, and increased risk across the growing LEO economy. The only operational system that characterizes this drag environment in real time is the Department of War’s (DoW) High Accuracy Satellite Drag Model (HASDM), which relies on an ad hoc collection of satellites and space debris tracked by ground radar. Its calibration data is unavailable to civil and commercial operators in real time and lacks the quality and timeliness needed for modern operations. This IRAD is designing the world's first purpose-built, openly licensed, GNSS (Global Navigation Satellite System)-enabled orbital drag calibration object constellation — small spacecraft with fully-characterized drag properties that deliver thermospheric density data at low latency, providing data that will enable space weather operators to improve on HASDM using openly-available data. The design is compatible with commercial CubeSat form factors and rideshare deployment, enabling a scalable constellation that can be manufactured, deployed, and operated by multiple civil and commercial parties. Critically, commercial operators can use these objects to characterize the drag environment near their own constellations without sharing proprietary spacecraft properties — the calibration object serves as an independent, openly documented reference.
benefits: World's first purpose-built, openly licensed, GNSS-enabled orbital drag calibration object constellation design; thermospheric density data at low latency; enables civil/commercial operators to improve on DoW HASDM using open data; compatible with commercial CubeSat form factors and rideshare deployment.

title: Fireproof Insulation for Resistive Environments in Materials for Aerospace and Navigation (FIREMAN)
lead_organization: Glenn Research Center (GRC) — Cleveland, Ohio
description: To create light-weight, thermally insulative, and mechanically robust materials that are fire resistant at high oxygen environments for enhanced crew and flight system safety in Mars habitats
benefits: Higher Martian gravity and more stringent planetary protection requirements poses unique challenges; Habitats in these conditions will demand different insulation protection than the current state of the art (SOA) materials available to the Artemis lunar crew. If successful, this project would help enable habitation off world with a new class of thermally insulating materials that can self-extinguish in the new Exploration Atmosphere. Benefits of which could prevent mission failure and increase safety to the crew.

title: Advanced Hybrid Composites for Aerospace Applications
lead_organization: Glenn Research Center (GRC) — Cleveland, Ohio
description: To develop hybrid carbon fiber polymer matrix composites (PMCs) for enhanced performance in extreme environments.
benefits: This effort seeks to combines the benefits of thermoplastic (TP) and thermoset (TS) composites with structural additives. The goal is to create more robust, light-weight materials with enhanced thermal and radiation stability, repairability, and a higher damage tolerance

title: Developing NEO Mass Measurement Capabilities for Planetary Defense
lead_organization: Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) — Greenbelt, Maryland
description: Asteroid mass is the single most important physical property for planetary defense, yet no existing space instrument or technique can measure it rapidly, accurately, and affordably during a high-speed flyby — a critical gap that limits NASA's ability to assess and respond to near-Earth object threats. To close this gap, Goddard is pursuing a coordinated two-pronged investment: PI Anand Mylapore is developing a miniaturized gravity gradiometer that directly measures an asteroid's gravitational gradient during a single close flyby, leveraging LISA Pathfinder heritage and University of Florida gravitational reference system technology to produce a validated instrument point design ready for infusion into a PDCO-funded rapid reconnaissance mission. Complementing this instrument development, PI Dakotah Rusley is advancing the TERP RAPTOR concept, developing flyby mass estimation algorithms and a maneuverable 12U CubeSat — built in partnership with the University of Maryland — that measures asteroid mass by precisely tracking differential spacecraft deflection using LIDAR ranging, targeting a factor-of-seven improvement over the current state of the art and a potential flight demonstration opportunity with AstroForge to the asteroid Apophis in 2028. Together, these two efforts form a strategically coordinated portfolio — one delivering the near-term demonstration capability, the other the long-term precision instrument — that positions Goddard to lead the next generation of planetary defense reconnaissance missions.
benefits: Two-pronged coordinated portfolio: (1) miniaturized gravity gradiometer (Mylapore) producing a validated instrument point design ready for infusion into a PDCO-funded rapid reconnaissance mission; (2) TERP RAPTOR (Rusley) — flyby mass estimation algorithms and a maneuverable 12U CubeSat measuring asteroid mass via LIDAR-based differential spacecraft deflection tracking, targeting 7× improvement over state of the art and a potential flight demonstration to asteroid Apophis in 2028 with AstroForge. Together: near-term demonstration capability + long-term precision instrument.

title: Maturation of the Lunar DustCam instrument for in situ monitoring of lunar dust
lead_organization: Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) — Greenbelt, Maryland
description: The proposed Lunar DustCam is a very low SWaP-C imaging system for in situ monitoring of sunlight scattered by naturally mobilized dust (e.g., from meteoroid impacts, electrostatic lofting and levitation) as well as “collateral” dust ejected by surface operations (e.g., lander plumes, astronaut and rover traverses, and ISRU). Lunar dust is known to be an exploration hazard on the Moon due to its deleterious effects on imaging systems, thermal radiators, and moving parts, such that characterizing dust transport is a critical requirement for safe operations. The Artemis III SDT report outlines the importance of real-time lunar dust monitoring and determination of dust accumulation on habitats, equipment, and optical surfaces. Development of Lunar DustCam will provide a critical capability needed for safe lunar surface operations during upcoming CLPS, Artemis, and Moon Base missions.
benefits: Very low SWaP-C imaging system for real-time monitoring of naturally mobilized and collateral lunar dust; dust transport characterization critical for safe surface operations; supports Artemis III SDT requirements for real-time dust monitoring and accumulation determination on habitats/equipment/optics.

title: Scalable Passive Interferometric Distributed Exploration Radiometer (SPIDER)
lead_organization: Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) — Greenbelt, Maryland
description: SPIDER will mature a distributed L-band interferometric radiometer architecture that uses 3D-printed antennas, coordinated/synchronized low-SWaP receiver nodes, and post-processed GNSS/SDR timing to synthesize large effective apertures without large deployable reflectors to improve passive microwave spatial resolution while enabling scalable hosted-payload and disaggregated observatory concepts. The FY27 effort will lay the technical foundation for a future LaRC sUAS multi-node demonstration by developing the system architecture, receiver-node concept, aperture-synthesis/RFI-geolocation algorithms, timing/baseline error budget, data-rate trade space, and 3D Printing of Electronics (3DPE) antenna approach, with hardware characterization and limited ground or single-node testing pursued as resources and schedule allow. The targeted infusion path is near-term Earth-science technology maturation for ESTO-relevant opportunities, airborne demonstrations, hosted-payload concepts, and disaggregated observatory architectures, with follow-on relevance to Heliophysics/space-weather sensing and Moon-to-Mars shallow-subsurface applications. As an Early-Stage Innovation, SPIDER is programmatically ambitious but technically conservative: FY27 will prioritize quantitative risk retirement before committing to a full multi-node moving-baseline demonstration.
benefits: System architecture for distributed L-band interferometric radiometer using 3D-printed antennas, low-SWaP receiver nodes, and GNSS/SDR timing; synthetic large effective apertures without large deployable reflectors; improved passive microwave spatial resolution enabling scalable hosted-payload and disaggregated observatory concepts.

title: FY27 CIF Dual Function Materials (DFM)
lead_organization: Ames Research Center (ARC) — Moffett Field, California
description: In order to develop a moon base for humans to live and mature technologies for humans to explore Mars, highly reliable life support systems with minimal size, weight, and power will be required. The longer humans are away from Earth, the more resource recycling will be required to maintain a habitable environment. Therefore, efficient closed-loop air revitalization systems are vital to crewed exploration mission success. The state-of-the-art closed-loop method requires multiple systems to dry the air, capture CO2, rehumidify the air, and convert the captured CO2 to water. A newly developed combination of sorbent and catalyst material called dual function materials (DFM) consolidates all of these systems into a single function, thereby greatly reducing the total size and weight of the air revitalization loop and saving millions of dollars in launch and operation costs. Use of DFM for this application is novel, so the optimal material formulation and lifetime must first be confirmed before development into a full system. Since DFM use a thermally driven packed bed, existing flight hardware can be directly utilized for rapid technology development. This proposed project aims to mature tailored, robust DFM for implementation into Moon Base and other exploration habitation architecture.
benefits: A newly developed combination of sorbent and catalyst material called dual function materials (DFM) consolidates all of these systems into a single function, thereby greatly reducing the total size and weight of the air revitalization loop and saving millions of dollars in launch and operation costs. Use of DFM for this application is novel, so the optimal material formulation and lifetime must first be confirmed before development into a full system. Since DFM use a thermally driven packed bed, existing flight hardware can be directly utilized for rapid technology development. This proposed project aims to mature tailored, robust DFM for implementation into Moon Base and other exploration habitation architecture.

title: Hot-Fire Demonstration of Cascading Rocket Nozzles
lead_organization: Stennis Space Center (SSC) — Stennis Space Center, Mississippi
description: The goal of project is to design a rocket engine nozzle that generates massive thrust in a tiny package. The cascade nozzles combine clustering and contouring to pack significant thrust in a petite package. They reduce inert vehicle mass that can be utilized for larger payloads and in various back pressure environments with a common design (i.e. Earth, Mars, in-space).
benefits: Simulations show ~50% increase in thrust at ~97.5% nozzle efficiency and ~15% bell-nozzle length. Drop in replacement nozzle for existing combustion devices.

title: H-MAST: Horizontal Multi‑Axis Shock Test
lead_organization: Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) — Huntsville, Alabama
description: Develop a system that performs simultaneous multi-axes response from a single impact event using an angled strike plate and cannon to split input energy equally across orthogonal axes.​
benefits: Simultaneous multi-axes response from a single impact event​ using an angled strike plate and cannon to split input energy equally across orthogonal axes​. Impact remains perpendicular to strike plate, eliminating shear effects and ensuring high fidelity and repeatable data​. Ability to test large test articles without shear induced fatigue​ onset from a single impact event​.

title: Advancement of eXploration Components for In-Space Servicing (AXCIS) Variable Output Regulator (VOR) Optimization
lead_organization: Kennedy Space Center (KSC) — Kennedy Space Center, Florida
description: The AXCIS Early Career Initiative (ECI) project developed a variable output regulator to technology readiness level (TRL) 4 for both low- and high-pressure servicing systems that allows for remote actuation over a large pressure range, enabling the ability to service multiple clients with one regulator in space or on the lunar/Martian surface. The AXCIS VOR Optimization project will perform work to raise the TRL of the AXCIS VOR to 6 through mechanical and electrical design optimization followed by delta qualification environmental testing.
benefits: A TRL 6 AXCIS VOR ready for space flight testing.

title: Resident Space Object Breakup Toolkit
lead_organization: Johnson Space Center (JSC) — Houston, Texas
description: Orbital Debris presents a significant risk to all Resident Space Objects (RSOs), including active spacecraft, and affects all historical, current, and future missions. The development of tools to characterize small debris in LEO and cis-lunar space is generally recognized as an important investment. The NASA Standard Satellite Breakup Model (SSBM) has been cited by over 750 works since 2001 and is the gold-standard for simulating on orbit-breakup events domestically and by ESA, CNES, JAXA, and many industry partners. However, it does not currently include the NASA Engineering Safety Center (NESC)-requested debris dependencies upon mass density (material) and debris shape—both significant risk drivers—or adequately reflect the dynamism of the orbital debris environment. This project addresses the shortfall and limitations of the 2001 SSBM by (1) developing a visualization toolkit for presentation to wider audiences and (2) conducting research and development efforts to facilitate updating the SSBM and ensuring its ability to be disseminated in the same fashion (and with the same impact) as the 2001 model. The new model will: -Include NESC requested mass density and fragment shape -Reflect the dynamic space economy and environment and be applicable to supporting (design, protection, operations) sustained cislunar orbital and surface activities -Be capable of publishing the model and disseminating it to the worldwide user community.
benefits: The team anticipates tools which draw from Probability Density Functions (PDFs) or similar analytical or semi-analytical functions and processes to characterize the multi-dimensional orbital debris fragment ensemble. In addition, hosting the web application for the greater public gives the global orbital debris community access to a validated satellite breakup model and accompanying analysis tools to complement the existing ORDEM (Orbital Debris Engineering Model) and DAS (Debris Assessment Suite) tools.

title: LuxBio Microgreens: De-Risking Autonomous Crop Phenotyping for Lunar Surface Food Production
lead_organization: Ames Research Center (ARC) — Moffett Field, California
description: NASA's Moon Base requires in situ fresh food production to provide crew nutrition and countermeasures against the vitamin degradation observed in pre-packaged space diets, necessitating cultivar screening on the lunar surface per NASA's Crop Readiness Level (CRL) 3 requirements. This proposal reframes Ames' flight-heritage BioSensor payload, enhanced with FY25/26 LuxBio multi-modal sensing, from an ISS-relevant testbed into a distributed lunar-surface network for autonomous crop cultivar selection. We propose to determine whether crop germination stage and seed vigor, a predictor of resilience, can be deduced from multispectral data. Using microgreens, ideal models that rapidly produce health-critical compounds (e.g., carotenoids, vitamin C), we will grow 16 promising cultivars in BioSensor fluidic cards within the LuxBio optical stack, collecting time-series 12-band spectral data (400–850 nm) alongside daily ground-truth germination-stage assessments over 14-day periods. We will produce characteristic spectra for each germination stage (ungerminated, radicle emergence, cotyledon emergence) using class mean spectra and Jeffreys-Matusita separability, develop a PLSDA classifier validated via confusion matrix, and quantify seed vigor through 14-day germination percentage and cotyledon-emergence uniformity. Supporting Moon-to-Mars Architecture goals (AS-5; TX06.3.5), success would position Ames with uniquely capable, flight-heritage hardware for autonomous cultivar screening across all Moon Base development phases.
benefits: The project will generate a time-series dataset of multispectral optical measurements from microgreen cultivars, annotated with germination stages and end-of-run germination percentages. Unique spectral signatures for each germination stage will be identified, enabling the development of a classification model to assess seed vigor and crop resilience. The partial least squares discriminant analysis (PLSDA) model aims for high accuracy in classifying germination stages, supporting autonomous crop screening for lunar food production. All datasets and analysis will be published in open-source repositories, with anticipated peer-reviewed publications and conference presentations. Ultimately, the work will advance flight-heritage hardware for reliable, in situ food production on the lunar surface, positioning Ames for future Moon Base missions

title: HEXITEC ASIC Pixelated CdTe Detector Front-End Electronics and Packaging Development
lead_organization: Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) — Huntsville, Alabama
description: Achieving high–angular resolution imaging in the hard X-ray bandpass requires continued advancement in pixelated detector readout technology. The HEXITEC ASIC CdTe pixel array, developed by Rutherford Appleton Laboratory, offers a uniquely capable detector architecture featuring an abuttable 80 by 80-pixel format with a 250 μm pitch, a full detector readout rate of 10 kHz, and an energy response spanning 2 to 200 keV. These performance characteristics make HEXITEC well suited for potential NASA Explorer class broadband X-ray space telescope mission concepts, including HEROIX. To enable these capabilities for spaceflight applications, further front-end electronics development is required. In parallel, dedicated packaging development is required to integrate the HEXITEC detectors into a flight like ready detector unit. This effort involves designing and validating mechanical, thermal, and electrical interfaces that ensure stable operation in the space environment. Key focus areas include temperature regulation for CdTe stability, low noise high voltage bias delivery. Establishing this packaging capability at MSFC will support end-to-end detector module development for upcoming mission proposals and technology maturation efforts. Calibration of the integrated HEXITEC detector units will also be performed at MSFC to establish detector gain and position sensitivity. Together, the proposed front-end electronics and packaging advancements will significantly enhance the readiness of HEXITEC detector technology, enabling high fidelity, high-resolution hard X-ray imaging for NASA’s next generation astrophysics missions. Not included in this IRAD, but required for high-resolution astrophysical application, is FPGA development. This includes implementing firmware capable of robust sparse event detection and rapid charge sharing characterization between adjacent pixels. Additional support will be required for final FPGA firmware for TRL 6.
benefits: Continued development of embedded hard X-ray detectors will directly complement MSFC's existing full-shell, high-angular resolution X-ray optics program, with advancements in HEXITEC development benefiting future MSFC-led missions including SuperHERO LDB (APRA/Pioneer), Next Generation ART-XC (Astro Tiny Explorer), FIRCE (Helio SMEX (GSFC)), and HEROIX (Astro MIDEX).

title: Miniaturized Gravity Gradiometer for Asteroid Mass Determination via Close Fly-By
lead_organization: Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) — Greenbelt, Maryland
description: We propose the development of a miniaturized gravity gradiometer for asteroid mass determination via close fly-by, leveraging deep-space flight heritage from the LISA Pathfinder (LPF) mission and combining two free-falling tungsten test masses with a laser ranging interferometer (LRI) to achieve gravity gradient sensitivity sufficient to survey a meaningful fraction of the accessible NEO population from a compact, self-contained instrument package. In partnership with the University of Florida, this IRAD will develop a comprehensive instrument error budget, conduct mission profile trade studies, and use the resulting preliminary instrument architecture as input to a focused point design study. The ultimate infusion target is a future directed or competed rapid NEO reconnaissance mission under the Planetary Defense Coordination Office (PDCO), directly responsive to the TRaHP Strategic Focus Area Pillar 3 call for novel mass-measuring approaches for an asteroid fly-by mission.
benefits: Comprehensive instrument error budget; mission profile trade studies; preliminary instrument architecture for compact gravity gradiometer using free-falling tungsten test masses and laser ranging interferometry; sensitivity sufficient to survey a meaningful fraction of accessible NEO population.

title: Adaptive Controls for Active Structural Controls
lead_organization: Armstrong Flight Research Center (AFRC) — Edwards, California
description: Continue parallel work with AFRL on rapid concept-to-wind tunnel testing​  -Conduct build-up flight experiments starting with rigid-wing vehicle​ ​  -Conduct powered flights with flexible-wing vehicle ​  -Develop initial adaptive control law strategies and test in tunnel/flight​  -Iterate on model/control design based on wind tunnel and flight datasets​
benefits: - Cost-effective way to gather flight data on relevant technologies in a limited envelope​  - Develop adaptive controls that make flight safer in the presence of plant/environmental uncertainties​  - Enable testing of complex/novel airframe configurations quickly​  - Validate autonomy-enabler tech​  - Testing advanced controllers for long, thin, high-aspect ratio wings a key to the design of future long-range (un)manned aerial vehicles and fuel-efficient transports​

title: Closed-Loop Machine Learning Framework for Accelerated Discovery of High-Performance Aerogel Composites
lead_organization: Glenn Research Center (GRC) — Cleveland, Ohio
description: To develop an AI-driven, closed-loop materials discovery framework that rapidly identifies and optimizes high-performance aerogel composites for next-generation spacecraft protection with fewer experiments, lower cost, and faster technology maturation
benefits: This effort will enable future of work possibilities and digital transformation to accurately predict high-performance formulations, enabling rapid, data-driven materials discovery with significantly fewer physical experiments.

title: Stereo PIV Study of Wake-Driven Dynamic Instability in Blunt Entry Vehicles
lead_organization: Langley Research Center (LaRC) — Hampton, Virginia
description: The project advances optical diagnostics for time resolved flow field measurements using 2D and Stereo PIV to study dynamic stability phenomena not captured by conventional methods. In FY26, we built a PIV system from the ground-up and brought the facility online. Success will deliver a scalable framework for EDL relevant aerodynamic and OML informed stability characterization.
benefits: Blunt body dynamic instability is danger to every EDL mission and instability is difficult to predict and mechanisms are poorly understood. This project aims to develop ability to identify dynamic stability concerns for new vehicle geometries during proposal phase. Improve data collection automation and processing for the new test setup, Synchronize PIV measurements with load cell data for detailed comparisons with VST, FDRF test data, Work towards developing on-body 3D PIV to capture full flow separatiottachment boundaries

title: Traction Enhancement Device for Robotic Excavation, Construction and Mining Platforms (TED)
lead_organization: Kennedy Space Center (KSC) — Kennedy Space Center, Florida
description: Provide a novel Traction Enhancement Device (TED) modular implement for the next generation excavator and mobility platforms, that will be used to meet NASA’s needs for lunar site preparation and construction with bulk regolith and rocks.
benefits: TRL 5 Proof of Concept Traction Enhancement Device (TED) establishing feasibility of providing enough enhanced traction to provide reaction force for regolith front end loader bucket and bulldozer implements and provide novel and superior slope climbing and descent capabilities. Enable higher-force excavation to allow larger regolith loads during operations, including the excavation and manipulation of large rocks and the ability to climb uphill slopes as steep as a 35 degree gradient and descend even steeper slopes, under control, on hills and craters.

title: Urine Stabilization and Toilet Improvement
lead_organization: Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) — Huntsville, Alabama
description: Recent events have shown the need for a simple, reliable urine stabilization method, along with a rethink of how NASA designs a space toilet. Promising results from a urine stabilization through resin test have opened a resin bed as a urine stabilization capability. The project would seek to expand the resin bed urine filtration testing and capabilities to figure out integration into Lunar systems. It would look at stabilization capabilities for short duration missions with urine storage, but also if a resin based toilet solution is possible. It would explore if, through a multi staged resin system, potable water could be created from raw urine.
benefits: If effective results are shown, a few hundred pounds of resin could replace approximately 1400 pounds of potable water for a 4 crew, 30 day mission through recycling. The system would cut down on significant launch mass if successful in consumable water usage by utilizing a short term regeneration system. The following KPPs are targeted: 1. Per NASA-STD-3001 V2: Bacterial Count < 50 CFU/ml, No detectable Coliform Bacteria per 100 ml, No detectable Fungal Count per 100 ml, and No detectable Parasitic Protozoa (e.g., Giardia and Cryptosporidium). 2. Conductivity: <1000 μS/cm (EPA recommendation) 3. Total Microbial growth: <50 CFU/ml

title: Compact Optical Method for Long-range, Inexpensive Network Communication (COMLINC)
lead_organization: Johnson Space Center (JSC) — Houston, Texas
description: COMLINC uses customized optics and Light Emitting Diodes (LEDs) to provide a dramatically lower SWaP-C system than the optical communications State of the Art. The first two years produced a low-cost optical ground station that can track a Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite and multiple prototype LED transmitters. One of the transmitters was launched into LEO during year 2 and will attempt to demonstrate a LEO downlink (increasing technology to TRL 6). During year 3, this project will further develop COMLINC technology by 1) developing uplink capability for COMLINC and 2) performing a trade study on potential applications of COMLINC with associated unit testing focusing on lunar surface conditions (e.g., dust, range, lighting, technology alternatives, etc.)
benefits: By adding uplink capability, COMLINC enables true bi‑directional optical communication at dramatically lower SWAP‑C than current state‑of‑the‑art optical systems. This approach can deliver data rates comparable to, or exceeding, traditional RF communications while avoiding RF‑spectrum regulatory constraints that significantly slow mission readiness timelines. Through targeted trade studies and unit testing under lunar‑relevant conditions, COMLINC can better define its operational envelope and mature into a low‑SWAP‑C architecture suitable for diverse lunar applications. Potential uses include communication among fixed lunar surface assets, mobile systems, and/or links between the lunar surface and Low Lunar Orbit (LLO).

title: System for Photogrammetric Imaging, Detection, and Ranging (SPIDR)
lead_organization: Kennedy Space Center (KSC) — Kennedy Space Center, Florida
description: SPIDR seeks to revolutionize camera tracking technology with a robust, modular, and autonomous system designed to support KSC launch/landing capture. Imagery systems play a vital role in assessing vehicle and GSE performance, detecting anomalies, and investigating incidents. The SPIDR project is being developed primarily to support Artemis launch tracking, in collaboration with the Exploration Ground Systems (EGS) program. The short-term goal of the project under FY27 IRAD is to deploy and integrate the SPIDR hardware at Pad 39B to autonomously track the Artemis III (or similar) launch. The future goal of the project is to expand SPIDR’s use-case to provide anomaly response and crew situational awareness capabilities, with the intent on developing SPIDR for the Moon Base.
benefits: SPIDR prototype demonstrated with Artemis III (or another launch from KSC)

title: Secure Autonomous Computing Stack
lead_organization: Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) — Greenbelt, Maryland
description: Objective: Deliver verified AI assurance methodologies that improve autonomous system quality and provide the confidence evidence required for mission-critical deployment of ASTRA capabilities. This initiative addresses the fundamental challenge that autonomous spacecraft operating in contested, delayed, and denied communication environments cannot depend on ground intervention when AI-driven decisions determine mission success. The proposed AI Assurance Framework provides the verification and validation foundation that makes trusted autonomy possible in safety-critical space applications. By establishing rigorous V&V methodologies specifically designed for AI's non-deterministic behaviors, we transform autonomous capabilities from promising technology demonstrations into mission-qualified systems. The proposed innovation develops a holistic assurance framework extending beyond traditional software assurance to encompass the entire AI system lifecycle. This includes robust requirements engineering for AI-based systems, specialized design assurance for non-deterministic behaviors, rigorous data governance protocols, continuous monitoring techniques, and AI-specific risk management strategies. To systematically improve AI system quality and establish mission confidence, we address critical research questions: What supplementary approaches beyond established V&V techniques guarantee consistent AI behaviors? How do we ensure continuous collection of accurate, complete data for AI monitoring and prediction? Are traditional safety envelopes sufficient, or do AI systems require alternative safety designs? How can Explainable AI and white-box analysis integrate into early development for formal verification? What methodologies validate "Double-AI" approaches where AI techniques verify AI systems? Direct Support for ASTRA Technology Pathways: This framework enables trust and certification for Trusted Autonomy and Resilience (verification for anomaly detection and self-healing), Autonomous Fault Detection, Isolation, and Recovery (safety envelopes for AI-driven fault response), and AI/ML-driven onboard science decision-making (explainable autonomous observation prioritization). This work addresses the confidence gap limiting AI infusion: stakeholders recognize autonomous capabilities' potential but lack assurance evidence for operational approval. We will continue coordinating with Code 700's CAIO to ensure institutional alignment, with IV&V to provide independent validation expertise for safety-critical operations, and with LaRC, ARC, and JPL research groups to leverage cross-center expertise in autonomous systems verification. Through rigorous synthesis of academic research, state of practice from other centers and agencies, and industry best practices, we will deliver a practical AI Assurance Framework addressing the unique challenges of opacity, emergent behaviors, and evolving capabilities in NASA's autonomous flight missions.
benefits: Holistic AI Assurance Framework for verification and validation (V&V) of autonomous spacecraft AI systems throughout the full lifecycle; rigorous V&V methodologies for non-deterministic AI behaviors; robust requirements engineering, design assurance, data governance, continuous monitoring, and AI-specific risk management; enables Explainable AI and white-box analysis integration; "Double-AI" validation methodologies; direct enablement of ASTRA Trusted Autonomy, Autonomous Fault Detection/Isolation/Recovery, and AI/ML-driven onboard science decision-making capabilities.

title: Advanced fiber optics for communications and sensing
lead_organization: Glenn Research Center (GRC) — Cleveland, Ohio
description: To leverage spatial mode diversity to increase bandwidth of communications and sensing systems
benefits: Design and prototype multimode chip coupler and multicore fiber launch. Low-power (Order of 1W) optical communications space transmitters limit deep-space range/data-rates (trade-off between peak power and rate). This effort will address this by designing multi-core fiber launch to spatially multiplex transmitter channels. Single mode photonic integrated circuits (PICs) have limited applicability to inherently multi-mode comm and sensing due to coupling challenge. This effort will address they by design multi-mode chip coupler.

title: MIDAS: Modular Interoperable Distributed Avionics and Software
lead_organization: Johnson Space Center (JSC) — Houston, Texas
description: Moon to Mars success will depend on government and industry partners delivering reliable systems within aggressive cost and schedule constraints. Avionics and software are critical enabling technologies for surface robotics, mobility systems, infrastructure, and spacesuits. However, bespoke electronics and control architectures slow iteration, increase integration burden, and amplify technical risk. MIDAS addresses this challenge through a catalog of modular, stackable hardware, firmware, and software building blocks. These low-cost, plug-and-play reference designs will accelerate future surface systems, improve maintainability, and mature critical control technologies towards a sustainable surface presence.
benefits: The project is expected to reduce avionics and software cost, schedule, and integration risk by providing reusable reference designs and a catalog of stackable hardware, firmware, and software building blocks for surface systems. Reprogrammable avionics, modular software, and reusable board designs will accelerate prototyping, simplify testing and troubleshooting, improve maintainability, and enable technologies to be adapted across spacesuits, satellites, robotic systems, rovers, science payloads, and surface infrastructure. Targeted use of radiation-tolerant and automotive-grade components could reduce avionics costs by up to 90 percent while maintaining appropriate reliability for a range of space applications. Publishing environmental test results for automotive-grade components will also reduce duplicated qualification efforts and help programs make more informed component-selection decisions. Together, these outcomes will help bootstrap commercial and government development of common products such as motor controllers and Ethernet switches while benefiting NASA, industry, defense, research institutions, and terrestrial users.

title: Enabling Niobium-based Alloy and Coating Technologies (ENACT)
lead_organization: Glenn Research Center (GRC) — Cleveland, Ohio
description: To develop, additively manufacture, and test oxygen-tolerant, hafnium-free niobium-based alloys and advanced coatings to enable higher temperature, more efficient, reusable reaction control system (RCS) thrusters
benefits: Design and manufacture a novel Nb alloy with advanced protective coating; Mitigate the NESC-identified flight safety risk ensuring reusability; Enable an increase in specific impulse by operating at > 1300°C

title: 5G Network Management for Lunar and Deep Space Communications
lead_organization: Glenn Research Center (GRC) — Cleveland, Ohio
description: To identify the essential network management functions for a successful lunar communication architecture by simulating how data traffic is automatically managed and protected over unreliable space connections leveraging terrestrial wireless technologies.
benefits: State of the art tools include modeling of lunar surface propagation, line of sight between assets, network traffic loading, and user data protocol simulation. They lack network performance monitoring and control functions. This project will assess network management protocol standards and extend the simulation framework to evaluate how they can be implemented in the end-to-end lunar network. Results will develop understanding of current 3GPP network management standards, enhance simulation tools for lunar scenarios and improve simulation fidelity of Moon Base end-to-end data flows.

title: LUNARMBENCH - Benchmarking Robotic Manipulation for Lunar Surface Logistics & Infrastructure
lead_organization: Ames Research Center (ARC) — Moffett Field, California
description: NASA’s Moon Base operations will require robotic systems to manipulate logistics items, payloads, cables, connectors, and infrastructure interfaces before crew arrival, during uncrewed periods, and alongside astronauts. At the same time, robotic manipulation is advancing rapidly through physical AI, learning-based control, improved simulation, and robot foundation models, but existing benchmarks remain largely terrestrial and do not evaluate the lunar-relevant tasks, interfaces, environmental stressors, or operational constraints NASA must understand. This CIF will establish LunArmBench, an Ames-led V0 benchmark and evaluation framework for lunar surface robotic manipulation. The project will translate Moon Base Autonomous Systems & Robotics capability targets into simulation-based benchmark tasks, focused on cable/connector mate-demate, cable handling/routing, logistics payload handling, and payload/interface alignment. The benchmark will define task protocols, manipulation primitives, scoring metrics, lunar-relevant stressors, and baseline evaluation methods. Using NVIDIA Isaac Sim/Isaac Lab and a low-cost bimanual manipulation platform, the team will produce initial simulation assets, benchmark specifications, baseline results, and a hardware validation roadmap. LunArmBench will provide Ames and NASA with reusable evaluation infrastructure to guide physical AI development, inform robot-compatible interface design, and support follow-on Moon Base robotics maturation.
benefits: The goal of LunArmBench is to establish an Ames-led V0 benchmark and evaluation framework for lunar surface robotic manipulation. LunArmBench will translate Moon Base manipulation needs into representative task definitions, manipulation primitives, simulation assets, scoring metrics, and baseline evaluations. The initial focus will be on three task families: cable/connector mate-demate and cable routing; logistics payload handling and staging; and payload/interface placement and alignment. Our hypothesis is that a compact, mission-grounded benchmark can provide actionable evidence about which robotic manipulation approaches, interfaces, and autonomy methods are most promising for lunar surface operations, while positioning Ames to lead a reusable evaluation capability for Moon Base physical AI.

title: SPOT: Single-Platform Object Triangulation for Air Domain Awareness
lead_organization: Langley Research Center (LaRC) — Hampton, Virginia
description: ARMD requires detecting/locating non-cooperative UAS for Air Domain Awareness. Current solutions rely on complex, multi-sensor or multi-vehicle solutions; a single standard UAS cannot easily achieve GPS-level 3D localization using it's pre-existing hardware. Target-agnostic 3D localization from one UAS requires solving complex issues: extracting accurate gimbal bearing measurements, integrating ML with triangulation, executing real-time geometric optimization, and operating on edge compute. SPOT is a hardware-agnostic, software-first architecture. While FY27 builds a modular payload as a testbench, the ultimate goal is an algorithmic suite that runs natively on any UAS equipped with a standard gimbaled camera and GPS.
benefits: This project aims to develop near GPS-grade 3D localization from a single platform with no ground infrastructure required. The target outcomes are to integrate ARL Archangel CV ML models for aerial human detection (proof-of-concept), calibrate and optimize gimbal for azimuth/elevation bearing measurement and center tracking, build end-to-end pipeline, and validate GPS-grade accuracy of 5m on static targets.

title: Deep Space and Moon Human Organoid Culture System
lead_organization: Ames Research Center (ARC) — Moffett Field, California
description: This proposal seeks to evolve ARC’s existing ISS Bioculture System (BCS) into spaceflight hardware for long-term biological culture and microscopic live imaging of human tissue organoids in Moon surface and Deep Space environments. This capability addresses a major human health knowledge gap for exploration science concerning how tissue-specific organoids respond to deep space radiation and altered gravity. This has not been adequately modeled by ISS experiments in LEO lacking the unique radiation quality and dose-rates characteristics of deep space, especially when combined with fractional or zero gravity. Key objectives are to design and prototype 1) a low-mass/volume Deep Space BCS based on modular components of the ISS BCS, and 2) a long-term microfluidic incubator for brightfield and epifluorescence microscopic imaging that can transmit data autonomously for up to one year without sample return. The technical approach repackages ISS BCS gas and power/control modules with a single cassette module with a microscopic imaging flow path, resulting in ~75% mass/volume/power reduction. This work strongly contributes to ARC leadership in developing Space Biosciences experimental capabilities for Moon Base and Moon-Mars Exploration, taking advantage of N288 Space Biosciences Collaborative technical, scientific, and engineering resources, aligning with NASA strategic goals of human Moon-Mars exploration and habitation.
benefits: The main goal in this proposal is to develop a novel Deep Space and Moon Human Organoid Culture System that can be used for generating new NASA science during Moon-Mars exploration to evaluate the combined partial/micro-gravity and elevated deep space radiation on human tissue organoid models.

title: Small All-range LIdar for Moon and Mars (SALI)
lead_organization: Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) — Greenbelt, Maryland
description: We propose to continue modifying our Small All-range LiDAR (SALI) to broaden its applications for the Moon to Mars program. We will continue the collaboration with the Goddard autoNGC team to develop a lower-cost version of SALI as an altitude sensor for lunar missions. We will build and test a 1.95-micron laser transmitter and conduct additional environmental test to SALI to further mature the instrument for a fast-track lunar or Mars mission.
benefits: Lower-cost SALI version as lunar altitude sensor; 1.95-micron laser transmitter build and test; additional environmental testing; broadened M2M program applications through GSFC autoNGC team collaboration.

title: SpaceVLA: Generalized Intelligent Autonomy for Space-Based Asset Decision-Making
lead_organization: Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) — Greenbelt, Maryland
description: My proposed work is to develop an integrated foundation-model and simulation infrastructure for autonomous operations in space-based environments, initially focused on lunar surface and Moon-base applications aligned with Artemis. The effort is two-fold, pairing (1) a pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model, which serves as the decision-making "brain" for assets such as rovers, landers, satellites, and robotic manipulators, with (2) a physics-grounded world model that provides a high-fidelity, interactive simulation environment for space-specific conditions. Unlike world models designed primarily around terrestrial environments, the space world model will represent mission-relevant factors such as lunar terrain and regolith, reduced gravity, illumination, thermal conditions, dust, sensor behavior and noise, communications, power, vehicle state, operational constraints, uncertainty, and faults. The VLA will be developed as a general pretrained model that downstream customers and stakeholders can fine-tune and post-train for their specific hardware, procedures, and objectives, then deploy within the world model to generate scenarios and synthetic training data, conduct reinforcement learning, and test and validate autonomous behaviors before flight. This workflow has produced state-of-the-art results and step-function gains in autonomy and efficiency across both autonomous driving and humanoid robotics, and preliminary research indicates it can be applied to space-based environments to greatly enhance autonomous operations. In addition to the models themselves, the work will establish reusable infrastructure, interfaces, and workflows that let NASA missions and both internal and external stakeholders adapt, evaluate, and deploy these capabilities for their own assets, creating a scalable autonomy foundation that can extend from lunar operations to Mars, orbital systems, and other deep-space environments. This effort is being pursued in collaboration with NVIDIA.
benefits: VLA model for autonomous decision-making in rovers, satellites, and landers; real-time autonomous mission operations without continuous Earth-based control; reinforcement learning-based refinement across diverse mission scenarios; establishes GSFC as the frontier center for space-based autonomy via ASTRA.

title: Pretreat-Safe Electrical Feedthrough
lead_organization: Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) — Huntsville, Alabama
description: Develop, manufacture, and test a pretreat-compatible electrical feedthrough that can safely breach layers the of containment required for ECLSS fluid systems, allowing system designers to put critical sensors and route power as close as possible to the underlying process.
benefits: At the end of this effort, we’ll have an electrical feedthrough that is materially-compatible, environmentally-tested, and ready for deployment in the next generation of ECLSS hardware.

title: Water vapor Infrared Sunlight Sounder with Photonic integrated circuits (WISSP)
lead_organization: Langley Research Center (LaRC) — Hampton, Virginia
description: WISSP aims to develop a photonic integrated circuit (PIC)-based spectrometer/polarimeter for measurement of the 3D distribution of water vapor from orbit. WISSP will be smaller and more accurate than current IR sounders, while providing cross-track coverage to supplement high-resolution lidar.
benefits: PIC technology enables CubeSat-sized instrument (3D maps + constellation). Develop, demonstrate, and characterize improved TRL 4 prototype suitable for brassboard implementation

title: FPGA-Accelerated Precision Time Protocol
lead_organization: Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) — Greenbelt, Maryland
description: This IRAD proposes to demonstrate an FPGA-accelerated implementation of Precision Time Protocol (PTP) v2.1 achieving sub microsecond accuracy for distributed spacecraft and lunar surface systems, addressing a critical gap in Earth-independent exploration infrastructure. Current approaches, Pulse-Per-Second (PPS) and Network Time Protocol (NTP), lack either absolute time distribution or necessary precision for autonomous coordination of distributed assets. PTP v2.1 delivers over 1000 times greater accuracy than NTP through hardware-timestamping at the physical layer, providing a robust timescale format with UTC offset support that enables Lunar Time Coordinated (LTC) distribution across lunar infrastructure. By developing flight-optimized FPGA components implementing frequency and phase correction in hardware, this effort establishes a reusable architecture deployable from individual spacecraft to distributed lunar networks, directly supporting ASSET Priority #5: "Exploration Enabling Systems" and enabling the sub microsecond time synchronization required for coordinated robotic operations, distributed sensor fusion, precision localization, and coordinated power distribution without Earth-in-the-loop commanding. Building on Goddard's heritage in flight-proven FPGA implementations and role in LCRNS architecture development, this IRAD matures precision timing capabilities essential for NASA's Ignition Initiative lunar surface operations, positioning Goddard as the center of excellence for timing infrastructure in Earth-independent exploration.
benefits: FPGA-accelerated PTP v2.1 achieving sub microsecond accuracy for distributed spacecraft and lunar surface systems; reusable architecture from individual spacecraft to distributed lunar networks; enables Lunar Time Coordinated (LTC) distribution across lunar infrastructure; >1000× greater accuracy than NTP.

title: Cross-Species Cardiac Digital Twin: Predicting Astronaut Myocardial Remodeling from Rodent & Stem-Cell Spaceflight Data
lead_organization: Ames Research Center (ARC) — Moffett Field, California
description: Cardiovascular deconditioning is a top-priority risk for long-duration exploration, yet the astronaut heart cannot be sampled in flight, so its mechanism is observable only in rodents and human stem-cell tissue. We will build and validate the founding computational module of a cross-species cardiac digital twin that predicts how an individual astronaut’s heart structurally remodels in spaceflight by translating mechanistic mouse and human engineered-cardiac-tissue data onto sparse human imaging. Cross-species translation is the core innovation, not a convenience: abundant rodent and stem-cell flight data are the only viable route to mechanistic, individualized human prediction. We will (1) curate an open, preservation-filtered, sex-stratified cross-species cardiac-spaceflight data package; (2) build a 3D finite-element cardiac growth-and-remodeling model with a calibrated unloading/atrophy branch plus a rapid surrogate for uncertainty quantification; (3) learn an explicit, pathway-level mouse-to-human mapping with allometric scaling; and (4) validate against analog and flight imaging and generate the first uncertainty-bounded counterfactual of regional cardiac remodeling for a Mars-transit profile under an ASME V&V40 context-of-use. The effort uses only existing open data, advances TRL 2→3 in one year, and converts data NASA already owns into a predictive capability it lacks.
benefits: We will build and validate the founding computational module of a cross-species cardiac digital twin that predicts how an individual astronaut’s heart structurally remodels in spaceflight by translating mechanistic mouse and human engineered-cardiac-tissue data onto sparse human imaging.

title: Cryogenic Capacitor Storage Module (CCSM)
lead_organization: Kennedy Space Center (KSC) — Kennedy Space Center, Florida
description: The goal is to integrate two KSC-developed technologies—CAPMAG and CFC—into a cryogenic prototype that functions as a low-pressure cryogenic gas storage and delivery system. Utilize aerogel rolled blankets embedded with metallic layers that serve a dual purpose: conducting heat to drive desorption of cryogenic fluid and function as capacitance plates for fluid mass sensing. This prototype will allow low pressure cryogenic storage, continuous liquid/mass quantity measurement and operate in microgravity (mitigate/eliminating sloshing) making it ideal for spaceflight and moon missions.
benefits: Demonstrated prototype cryogenic capacitor storage module that will allow low pressure cryogenic storage, continuous liquid/mass quantity measurement and operate in microgravity (mitigate/eliminating sloshing) making it ideal for spaceflight and moon missions.

title: LUCID: Lunar Clean ISRU Depot
lead_organization: Kennedy Space Center (KSC) — Kennedy Space Center, Florida
description: The overarching goal of this project is to enable sustainable human presence and technical operations on the Moon with production of clean, usable lunar oxygen. Specifically, the project aims to advance in-situ resource utilization (ISRU) capabilities by developing and validating a small-scale system capable of purifying raw, mixed gas produced through Molten Regolith Electrolysis (MRE) and similar systems which will require gas purification. The primary objective is to design and test a small-scale cryocooler separation unit—incorporating a heat exchanger and refrigerant loop—based on the method selected by the C3PO trade study. The system must successfully isolate oxygen from the MRE output gas by precisely regulating temperatures, while concurrently filtering out solid impurities such as soot and regolith dust. Furthermore, the project aims to verify that the system can consistently meet strict end-use purity thresholds, specifically targeting breathing-grade oxygen at 99.0% to 99.5% purity (with a maximum of 50 ppm of water) and Grade F oxygen at 99.995% purity for specialized technical work, research, and welding.
benefits: This technology will provide a highly robust, dust-resilient (ISRU) system capable of continuously producing propellant-grade and life-support oxygen for lunar and Martian missions by coupling Molten Regolith Electrolysis (MRE) or like system with cryogenic fractional distillation.

title: Assessment of Quantum Enhanced Fiber Optic Gyroscopes for NASA Moon to Mars Missions
lead_organization: Glenn Research Center (GRC) — Cleveland, Ohio
description: To determine whether quantum‑enhanced (QE) Fiber Optic Gyroscopes (FOGs) can close identified gyro‑performance gaps for lunar landing and optical communications by quantifying those gaps, comparing classical and quantum options, validating key performance mechanisms through laboratory rotation testing, and identifying TRL‑limiting barriers.
benefits: This effort seeks to provide a clear understanding of the performance levels required for fiber‑optic gyroscopes in lunar landing and deep‑space optical communication systems, along with an assessment of where quantum‑enhanced architectures can realistically meet those demands. By quantifying key performance tradeoffs and identifying any gaps or TRL‑limiting factors, the project will establish the technical basis needed to guide the next stage of development, such as targeted component improvements or benchtop validation campaigns.

title: Development of Terahertz Single-Photon Detectors Based on Hafnium-Aluminum Transmon Resonator Qubits for Future NASA Far-Infrared and Submillimeter Missions
lead_organization: Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) — Greenbelt, Maryland
description: The exploration of the far-infrared (FIR) and terahertz (THz) spectral regimes remains one of the highest priority frontiers in modern astrophysics, planetary science, and Earth observation. Observations in this wavelength range are critical for tracing the cosmic history of star formation, probing the interstellar medium, characterizing the atmospheres of outer planets, and monitoring Earth’s atmospheric composition. However, realizing the full scientific potential of future NASA flagship and probe-class space observatories demands revolutionary leaps in detector sensitivity. Current state-of-the-art technologies, such as Transition Edge Sensors (TES) and Microwave Kinetic Inductance Detectors (MKIDs), are rapidly approaching fundamental noise limits. To surpass these limitations and achieve true background-limited performance or single-photon counting capabilities in the THz regime, novel detection paradigms must be explored. This FY26 Small Scale Strategic Technology Development IRAD proposes the design, fabrication, and cryogenic characterization of an ultra-sensitive, quantum-coherent THz single-photon detector based on transmon resonator qubits. Building upon recent breakthroughs in superconducting quantum information science and adapting mechanisms detailed in recent literature (e.g., arXiv:2601.16261 and arXiv:2103.06803), we propose a hybrid superconducting architecture that seamlessly integrates a broadband THz antenna with a highly sensitive qubit-based readout. The proposed detector architecture consists of a macroscopic Aluminum (Al) superconducting film that serves a dual purpose: it acts as a broadband antenna tailored to couple incident THz radiation, and it functions as the primary absorber. At the heart of the antenna structure lies a nanoscale Hafnium (Hf) Josephson junction, which provides the nonlinear inductance characteristic of a transmon qubit. The choice of materials is highly deliberate and leverages the superconducting gap engineering principle. Because Hafnium possesses a significantly lower superconducting energy gap compared to Aluminum, it naturally creates a potential well for quasiparticle dynamics. The operational principle of the proposed detector is fundamentally distinct from standard calorimetric or kinetic inductance methods. When a THz photon is successfully coupled into the Aluminum antenna structure, its energy is absorbed, breaking Cooper pairs and generating a cascade of nonequilibrium quasiparticles. Because of the engineered superconducting gap gradient between the Al film and the Hf junction, these quasiparticles rapidly diffuse toward the center of the structure where they become deeply trapped in the lower-gap Hafnium film. Once trapped within the localized Hf region, these quasiparticles tunnel across the Josephson junction. This localized quasiparticle tunneling dynamically alters the quantum state and the effective Josephson inductance of the transmon circuit. Because the junction is embedded within a microwave superconducting resonator, this shift in the nonlinear inductance translates directly into a dispersive shift of the structure’s resonant frequency. By capacitively coupling this transmon resonator to a standard microwave transmission line, we can continuously monitor the phase and amplitude of a microwave probe tone. A single THz photon absorption event will therefore register as a discrete, measurable quantum jump in the microwave readout signal. This coherent, non-dissipative readout mechanism isolates the fragile quantum sensor from amplifier noise, theoretically allowing for unprecedented Noise Equivalent Power (NEP) and resolving individual THz photons with high fidelity. During this FY26 IRAD effort, our team will execute a rapid, small-scale technology maturation plan consisting of three primary phases: (1) Electromagnetic and quantum circuit co-design to optimize the broadband Al antenna coupling and Hf junction parameters for maximal THz absorption and readout fidelity; (2) Nanofabrication of the hybrid Al/Hf transmon structures utilizing the advanced lithography and thin-film deposition capabilities at GSFC’s detector development facilities; and (3) Ultra-low temperature (millikelvin) dilution refrigerator testing to characterize the device’s dark count rates, quasiparticle lifetimes, and response to heavily attenuated thermal THz sources. Successful demonstration of this transmon-based detector concept will establish a foundational capability at NASA Goddard Space Flight Center for quantum-enhanced electromagnetic sensing. By transitioning qubit architectures from quantum computing applications into the realm of astronomical instrumentation, this IRAD will uniquely position GSFC to lead the development of next-generation focal plane arrays. The scalability of the microwave multiplexing readout inherent to transmon resonators further ensures that this technology can eventually be expanded into large-format arrays, directly aligning with the strategic technology needs of NASA’s future FIR/THz space missions.
benefits: Design, fabrication, and cryogenic characterization of ultra-sensitive THz single-photon detector; unprecedented Noise Equivalent Power (NEP) and individual THz photon counting; foundational quantum-enhanced electromagnetic sensing capability at GSFC; scalable microwave multiplexing readout for large-format focal plane arrays.

title: Fuel-Rich Gas Generator Vacuum Testing to Validate Performance Improvements (FRiGG)
lead_organization: Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) — Huntsville, Alabama
description: Recent testing at MSFC yielded unexpected results for gaseous oxygen and gaseous methane (GOx-GCH4) combustion systems.
