Measured combustion temperatures exceed theoretical chemical equilibrium predictions, contrasting with historical liquid-liquid propellant behavior falling below equilibrium. Combustion temperatures appear agnostic to injector type. These findings warrant validation through an independent test effort with a traceable thrust measurement system. Applications include, but are not limited to, Reaction Control System (RCS) thrusters.
benefits: The proposed work is expected to deliver several high value outcomes that advance both propulsion science and permeable additive manufacturing technologies: - Mission or Program value: The outcomes support architectures requiring reliable, high performance RCS systems. - Science and Engineering Improvements: The effort addresses key unknowns in combustion physics and materials development. New datasets will refine equilibrium performance models for methane–oxygen systems, improving prediction accuracy and informing future engine design. - Risk Reduction or Infusion Potential: This work reduces technical risk for future missions that may rely on RCS systems or thermal management solutions that have the potential to increase hardware life with improved cooling and propellant dispersion for increased combustion efficiency.

title: QTWTT as the Quantum Metrology Overlay for LunaNet Time-Scale Interoperability
lead_organization: Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) — Greenbelt, Maryland
description: Future lunar missions will need a dependable way to keep Moon-based time connected to Earth-based time. Radio and optical methods will provide the main operational links, but NASA will also benefit from an independent, high-confidence quantum method that can verify and calibrate the relationship between Coordinated Lunar Time and UTC/TAI. This study explores whether quantum two-way time transfer can become that added layer of confidence for LunaNet and LCRNS.
benefits: A practical go/no-go feasibility study determining whether quantum two-way time transfer can serve as an independent, high-confidence verification and calibration layer between Coordinated Lunar Time (LTC) and UTC/TAI; development of a mission concept, timing model, link budget, and demonstration roadmap for a compact quantum timing payload on a future lunar relay or surface node; enhanced robustness of lunar navigation, communications, science measurements, and multi-provider time interoperability as NASA builds sustained Moon-to-Mars infrastructure. Low-cost approach leverages existing GSFC/NIST quantum time-transfer results — no flight hardware required.

title: Leveraging AI-Driven Methodologies to Enable Sun-to-Earth Space Weather Modelling
lead_organization: Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) — Greenbelt, Maryland
description: One of the major challenges in space weather modeling is the computationally prohibitive range in scales between small pre-eruptive features and the large scale of the heliosphere. The computational challenge results in large-scale simulations typically either under-resolving the solar structures giving rise to space weather or being forced to contend with a numerical boundary condition in the solar corona, resulting in a substantial physical impact on the evolution of the simulation. This boundary condition is particularly daunting as observational constraints on the magnetic topology are notoriously difficult to directly obtain in the solar corona. Our proposed innovation is to replace this poorly constrained boundary condition with an AI emulation trained on a suite of simulations of solar eruptions. IRAD investment in this project will strengthen a proposed NASA/Department of Energy partnership through the Argonne National Laboratory Leadership Computing Facility’s AI Program for EXploration (APEX).
benefits: AI emulation of poorly-constrained solar coronal boundary conditions, trained on solar eruption simulation suite; eliminates under-resolved solar structures and uncertain numerical boundaries; computationally efficient Sun-to-Earth space weather simulation capability.

title: Glenn Regolith Composites for Sustainable Lunar Operations and Presence in Extreme Environments (GRC-SLOPEE)
lead_organization: Glenn Research Center (GRC) — Cleveland, Ohio
description: To develop fiber reinforced lunar regolith-based geopolymer composite that is light weight, fire-, heat- and radiation-resistant with high strength >100 MPa utilizing 70-90% in-situ resources (ISRU) and minimum of earth sourced materials and water.
benefits: Develop high temperature >600°C and strength >100MPa regolith-based composite utilizing 70% ISRU materials. Create surfaces and structures that enable maximum crew mobility and safety and mission success

title: Lunar Glovebox Development
lead_organization: Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) — Huntsville, Alabama
description: This effort will identify technologies in current, operational gloveboxes that can be upgraded. Targeted improvements will be efficiency, sound levels, and power consumption. Additional goals will be to reduce the overall complexity, and thereby the system requirements, while maintaining essential safety and performance. This will improve reliability and ensure levels of containment remain if a system fails.
benefits: A glovebox system with reduced complexity and improved efficiency. This will enable operation across a broader range of vehicles while allowing users to conduct activities in an isolated, dust-free volume.

title: MR Vision_Micro-Radar Vision System for Planetary Navigation & Hazard Detection
lead_organization: Ames Research Center (ARC) — Moffett Field, California
description: The “MR Vision” project will demonstrate how mm-wave radar can enable autonomous navigation for planetary mobility. In this project, we will integrate the Aloft “micro-Radar Vision System” (µRVS) with the K-REX2 planetary rover and assess navigation capabilities in the Roverscape. The µRVS is the size of a smartphone and derives from automotive radar components. K-REX2 has been used for many planetary analog tests and VIPER navigation engineering. The planned tests will leverage new K-REX2 software and infrastructure being developed for the RTMD “LIDAR LAUNCHER” project. Radar is widely used by the autonomous vehicle industry but has yet to be applied to planetary mobility. Radar can overcome limitations of cameras and lidar, particularly in difficult lighting conditions and when there are obscurants, such as dust. Moreover, radar combined with interferometry algorithms can provide accurate localization, hazard detection, and terrain mapping.
benefits: Demonstrate a navigation sensor that performs well independent of environmental lighting, that can robustly detect obstacles and terrain hazards (including negative features), and that facilitates both absolute and relative localization

title: Characterizing Cathode Current Dynamics to Reduce High Voltage Transients in Hall Thrusters
lead_organization: Glenn Research Center (GRC) — Cleveland, Ohio
description: To investigate and mitigate the root cause of damaging electrical spikes during Hall thruster operation.
benefits: Hall Effect Thruster (HET) cathodes produce high-voltage transients that can damage the propulsion string and the spacecraft. This effort seeks to determine the contributing factors through a parametric study and incorporate findings into future designs that do not produce high voltages.

title: Quantum Frequency Converter (QFC)
lead_organization: Glenn Research Center (GRC) — Cleveland, Ohio
description: To develop a quantum frequency converter to interconnect microwave and optical qubits while preserving quantum states
benefits: Superconducting microwave qubits are the most widely used implementation of quantum computation – but networking over long distances is challenging due to thermal noise and attenuation. Transmission of quantum states over optical channels can be done over long distances without such degradations. Bidirectional optical/microwave quantum conversion is required to interface microwave quantum processors with optical transmission systems

title: Mars Scoreboards
lead_organization: Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) — Greenbelt, Maryland
description: To safeguard Mars crewed and robotic missions, the Community Coordinated Modeling Center (CCMC) is developing capabilities to model, predict, and display space weather at Mars. We will develop a new Mars Solar Irradiance scoreboard and continue the development of the Mars Coronal Mass Ejection (CME) and Solar Energetic Particle (SEP) Scoreboards. We will enable both real-time forecasts and science hindcast simulations of the Mars environment using the Mars-BATSRUS (magnetosphere and ionosphere, M/I) and the Mars-GITM (thermosphere and atmosphere, T/A) models. This will be the first major step towards building real-time space weather situational awareness at Mars.
benefits: New Mars Solar Irradiance Scoreboard; continued Mars CME and SEP Scoreboards development; real-time forecasts and science hindcast simulations of the Mars environment; first major step toward real-time space weather situational awareness at Mars.

title: Advancing the State of the Art in Space Weather Modelling with in-situ Data Driving
lead_organization: Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) — Greenbelt, Maryland
description: Self-consistent and observationally driven modeling of space weather impacts the whole way from the solar photosphere to sites of human presence in the heliosphere is a powerful tool in protecting our astronauts and satellites in space and our technologies on the ground. This proposal advances two key aspects of the ingestion of data into numerical simulations to enable this technology. First, we will generate a pipeline to make self-consistent photospheric datasets from the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager on NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory to provide complete and comprehensive constraints for the time dependent evolution of all plasma properties at the solar photosphere, thereby advancing our knowledge of the initiation of space weather. Second, we will mature an innovative new technique for including the input of in-situ measurements from current and future satellites orbiting the Sun, the Earth-Sun L1 point, and the Mars-Sun L1 point to provide important validation, correction, and cleaning of the modelled impacts before their arrival at Earth, the Moon, and Mars.
benefits: Self-consistent photospheric datasets from SDO/HMI; pipeline for ingesting in-situ measurements from current and future solar/L1/Mars-L1 satellites; improved validation, correction, and cleaning of modeled space weather impacts before arrival at Earth, Moon, and Mars.

title: The SHADOW Digital Twin (Supervisory Human Analog for Decision-making and Operational Work-state)
lead_organization: Langley Research Center (LaRC) — Hampton, Virginia
description: With Mars one-way comms delays up to 22 minutes, flight crew are the safety-critical layer, supervising highly automated systems without real-time ground support. Yet routine monitoring demands little attention, and planners cannot verify if a crew member is engaged. Current digital twins replicate vehicles and habitats, not the crew supervising them. A credible digital twin requires bidirectional coupling, real-time state synchronization, and predictive projection to the host system. Hardware state is directly measurable, whereas cognitive readiness must be inferred from non-invasive signals alone. SHADOW must start generalizable and tune to a specific crew member, a dual constraint that strains models built for one or the other. Meeting that bar gives each astronaut a uniquely calibrated twin. This project aims to operationalize human performance science by fusing bottom-up non-invasive sensors (eye tracking, overt behavior) with top-down theory. Bidirectionally coupled to the host system, it infers readiness, synchronizes state in real time, and feeds projections back.
benefits: For future Mars missions with Mars comms delays up to 22 min crew will supervise automation with no real-time ground support. The approach in this project to enable technology/methods that frames human as resilient layer, not a failure source in such scenarios. Target outcomes include: Generalizable base model from non-invasive inputs (eye tracking, overt behavior), Finite state machine then hidden Markov model developed to classify engaged vs. displaced attention

title: Elastocaloric Solid-state Thermal Regulation for Astronauts (ELASTRA)
lead_organization: Glenn Research Center (GRC) — Cleveland, Ohio
description: To explore a new highly-efficient cooling technology, known as the elastocaloric effect (eCE) in shape memory alloys (SMAs), to support future space missions.
benefits: ELASTRA aims to develop solid state cooling by employing mechanical torsion in SMA tubes to drive the eCE instead of compression or tension, which have already been extensively investigated in prior work. This work will develop a system test-bed of effective scaling methods and optimal tube geometries for higher cooling rates.

title: An AI/ML approach to detection of launch and orbital debris in the upper atmosphere
lead_organization: Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) — Greenbelt, Maryland
description: We propose developing an AI/ML feature detection framework for detecting mesospheric aerosols, including plumes from rocket launches, to be initially applied to the Ozone Mapping Profiler Suite-Limb Profiler (OMPS-LP) dataset. The framework will be applicable and enhancing to upcoming NASA missions (e.g., the NASA Stratosphere Troposphere Response using Infrared Vertically-resolved light Explorer, STRIVE). The output dataset of mesospheric aerosol perturbations will be available for use in Earth system models to assess radiative and chemical impacts of these increasingly frequent events, as well as more generally to the research, defense, and intelligence communities to observe and study the impacts of upper atmospheric perturbations on radiation propagation relevant to communication and guidance systems.
benefits: AI/ML feature detection framework for mesospheric aerosols/rocket plumes using OMPS-LP; output dataset of mesospheric aerosol perturbations usable in Earth system models; assessment of radiative and chemical impacts of increasingly frequent launch events.

title: Inferring Solar Coronal Currents to Determine the Origins of Space Weather
lead_organization: Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) — Greenbelt, Maryland
description: We propose to develop an observational tool that will allow us to predict the onset of eruptions using solar surface vector magnetograms, or any future vector magnetograms in the solar atmosphere, by targeting the cause of the eruptions: the electric currents that build up in the solar atmosphere. Our approach utilizes expertise and existing tools at GSFC and will produce an analysis tool that can be run on existing and future NASA satellite asset data to infer when these electric currents build up prior to eruption. This vital piece in the chain of information needed to develop accurate space weather will provide predictive capabilities and also the initial conditions for space weather models, which are necessary for human DNA technological exploration of our solar system.
benefits: Observational analysis tool predicting solar eruption onset using surface vector magnetograms; inference of electric current buildup prior to eruption; vital initial conditions for space weather models; improved predictive capabilities for human and technological exploration.

title: Weather-driven Hazard Assessment of Lunar Electrodynamics (WHALE)
lead_organization: Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) — Greenbelt, Maryland
description: The lunar south pole, where future human missions are planned, is an unexplored terrain with unknown risks. Among the many potential hazards facing astronauts during lunar south pole exploration, tribocharging has been identified by NASA’s EVA and Human Surface Mobility (EHP) program as a high-priority 5×5 risk. As astronauts walk, work, or traverse the lunar surface, contact electrification can occur between spacesuits, tools, vehicles, and the regolith due to charge accumulation. Assessing the surface electrodynamics including the self-consistent plasmas is thus critical to the safety of human and robotic explorers to the Moon. The proposed innovation, Weather-driven Hazard Assessment for Lunar Electrodynamics (WHALE), will quantify for all possible lunar environment (1) surface electric potentials and the corresponding plasma populations, and (2) Intense charging caused by energetic particles in addition to their known radiation damage. WHALE will integrate a high volume of advanced three-dimensional simulations with machine learning to produce real-time surface charging forecasts that can be displayed on a hand-held device. Results of WHALE’s initial phase will guide the determination of instrument specifications (such as energy range, energy resolution, size of electric probes, and placement) for GSFC’s Plasma Observatory for Lunar Exploration mission to be delivered to EHP in April 2027.
benefits: Quantify surface electric potentials and plasma populations across all possible lunar environments; characterize intense charging from energetic particles; integrate 3D simulations with ML for real-time surface charging forecasts on handheld devices; guide instrument specifications for GSFC's Plasma Observatory for Lunar Exploration (POLE) by April 2027.

title: Battery Thermal Runaway Simulating Chemical Igniter
lead_organization: Johnson Space Center (JSC) — Houston, Texas
description: Human rated batteries must undergo thermal runaway propagation testing, in which a single cell in the battery is sent into thermal runaway to determine the severity of such a failure and if loss of vehicle/crew could occur. NASA does not have a gold-standard method of ignition that does not result in bias to the system due to the damage required of a live cell, resulting in lower confidence about test success and an inability to quantify margins effectively. The Lithium Ion Cell Simulating Chemical Igniter aims to standardize one or more classes of easily triggerable chemical igniters sized to replace a cell in a battery block. Such an igniter could reproduce the total ejected energy and timescale of a typical cell in a highly repeatable fashion, enabling a common test article for battery certification. This technology will allow commercial partners and NASA programs to easily define success and evaluate margins of safety.
benefits: This technology addresses the architectural need for a more standardized and rigorous thermal runaway propagation test. Such a device (or series of devices) will allow a common scoring method for anticipated energy, and survival at each level of initiator will give confidence in safety margins of battery units under test. It will also allow battery designs from entirely different systems and manufacturers to be fairly compared to one another. This technology will be broadly applicable to any commercial industry (e.g. automotive, aerospace, etc.) performing their own thermal runaway testing and would likely result in patent and commercial licensure, along with generally strengthening NASA’s leadership in the battery safety sector. In addition, it will also be utilized by other government agencies who build and test battery systems for use in their systems.

title: Radiation-Aware Edge AI for Future Space Nuclear and Surface Autonomy Systems: Inference Fidelity Characterization on Rad-Tolerant FPGA Platforms
lead_organization: Glenn Research Center (GRC) — Cleveland, Ohio
description: To quantify how Machine Learning (ML) inference accuracy degrades under cumulative radiation dose (TID) on NASA’s next-generation edge computing platforms — RTG4 rad-tolerant FPGA, PIC64-HPSC, and EdgeCortix SAKURA-II — to enable trustworthy onboard autonomy.
benefits: Measured dose margins for trusting onboard AI: informs FDIR design and platform selection for nuclear and surface autonomy missions; First inference fidelity data on NASA's next flight computing, ahead of 2027 HPSC flight silicon

title: Matrixed Autonomous Knowledge Orchestrator (MAKO)
lead_organization: Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) — Huntsville, Alabama
description: MAKO is an initiative to develop, evaluate, and deploy a general-purpose autonomous agent framework. It is designed to execute complex, repetitive, and safety-critical technical workflows within the mission analysis ecosystem. MAKO aligns with the goal of advancing autonomous systems, intelligent system health management, fault management automation, and AI-assisted mission operations.
benefits: Execute Autonomously: The framework will reliably perform complex, repetitive, and safety-critical workflows such as risk modeling, Monte Carlo evaluations, and fault-management testing without requiring constant human orchestration. (Additional tool incorporation can be established if/when needed) Operate Securely and Offline: The system will function entirely on-premise, ensuring data security and offline capability (when needed). Connection to NASA network will be needed to allow for downloading of external open-source data, software, and models. Interpret Intent and Manage Tasks: The framework will be able to translate high-level user goals into concrete, executable procedures, manage computational resources effectively, and produce accurate, verifiable results. Additionally, framework will be developed to utilize internal NASA analysis tools and applications. Enhance Efficiency: It is expected to significantly reduce analyst time and schedule friction associated with high-volume analytical processes. Strategic Alignment: This project will help establish the SHARC Lab as a center for agent-driven mission automation.

title: Fiber Laser Source for Ultracold Cesium-based Quantum Applications
lead_organization: Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) — Greenbelt, Maryland
description: We propose to develop an in-house fiber optic laser amplifier to generate 852 nm light for quantum applications involving ultra-cold cesium atoms. Lasers employed for these ultracold quantum applications require high frequency stability, narrow spectral bandwidth, excellent tuning precision, and high output power. An all-fiber optic laser system is the preferred architecture over existing free space systems because of its immunity to mechanical perturbations and thermal swings, high electrical efficiency, Telecordia-qualified parts, and substantial wavelength tunability. For the proposed effort, we will demonstrate >20 dB of optical gain at 852 nm in a single-stage erbium-doped ZBLAN fiber amplifier and demonstrate further scalability to >10 W.
benefits: >20 dB optical gain at 852 nm in single-stage ZBLAN fiber amplifier; scalability to >10 W output; all-fiber architecture with immunity to mechanical/thermal disturbances.

title: Wayfinding and Infrastructure Routing Experiment (WIRE)
lead_organization: Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) — Huntsville, Alabama
description: Develop and demonstrate autonomous capabilities for deploying, recovering, and burying proxy power/data cables in a lunar analog environment using LiDAR-equipped rovers.
benefits: Knowledge and algorithms for the autonomous deployment of cable infrastructure.

title: An intuitive toolkit for monitoring global HF radio signal interference in ionospheric E- and F-layers to support space weather modeling
lead_organization: Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) — Greenbelt, Maryland
description: We propose a technology development to deliver a benchmark product of near-real-time, globally integrated maps detailing amplitudes and occurrences of scintillations utilizing GNSS radio occultation measurements from the operating satellite constellation COSMIC-2. These scintillations represent consequential risks for terrestrial resources and NASA’s Moon to Mars architecture. To achieve the proposed goal, the project will build an automated software package to facilitate the effective ingestion, processing, and visualization of LEO-GNSS satellite data. This innovation is based on developing a novel technology of processing those near-real-time observations from satellite constellations. The outcomes of this effort will address the urgent operational need of situational awareness of the interferences of radio signals due to scintillations. This project will provide the foundational technology for future commercial data streams, supporting a game-changing capability for near-Earth modeling, operations, and research.
benefits: Near-real-time, globally integrated maps of GNSS scintillation amplitudes/occurrences using COSMIC-2; automated software for LEO-GNSS data ingestion, processing, and visualization; improved situational awareness of radio signal interference risks to terrestrial and space assets.

title: SENTRY-Mars: Solar, Environment, and iNterplanetary dynamics Tracking and Response sYstem at Mars.
lead_organization: Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) — Greenbelt, Maryland
description: The FY26 IRAD laid the groundwork in observation prioritization for SENTRY-Mars, this follow-on IRAD will mature the Mars-Sun L1 mission concept toward a closed, architecture-ready capability that can support future Moon-to-Mars infrastructure. Building on the FY26 Mars L1 space weather (SWx) IRAD and expanding to include Mars weather (MWx), SENTRY-Mars will define a digitally designed, uncertainty-aware observatory that couples direct solar (e.g., upstream solar wind, SEP/CME) and radiation monitoring with full-disk Martian atmospheric observations. The result will be a traceable mission architecture for actionable environmental intelligence that supports crew safety, EDL, communications, power, ISRU, EVA, and robotic operations at Mars.
benefits: Mature Mars-Sun L1 mission concept toward closed, architecture-ready capability; digitally designed uncertainty-aware observatory coupling solar/radiation monitoring with full-disk Martian atmospheric observations; traceable mission architecture supporting crew safety, EDL, communications, power, ISRU, EVA, and robotic operations at Mars.

title: Deployable Membrane Optical Communication System
lead_organization: Langley Research Center (LaRC) — Hampton, Virginia
description: DEMONS is a novel approach to spaceborne laser communication using membrane optics. The mass/volume of traditional optics has confined spaceborne laser communication to one-off demonstration missions at considerable cost with no path for large scale adoption. Once successful, DEMONS will enable low-cost scalable communication throughout the solar system to replace the Deep Space Network.
benefits: Advance light-weight deployable optics technology for future space laser communication. Demonstrate membrane optical receivers between 15 km and 50 km on a high-altitude balloon, Develop point design for a spaceborne technology demonstration mission

title: AXIS: Advancing X-ray Instrumentation in Space
lead_organization: Johnson Space Center (JSC) — Houston, Texas
description: NASA is dramatically increasing its Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) cadence as part of the Ignition initiative to support a permanent Moon Base. NASA is looking for low-cost, high-TRL instruments to fly on these CLPS landers. This IRAD project advances the TRL of a COTS X-ray fluorescence spectrometer (XRF) through testing components under lunar-relevant thermal and pressure conditions, as well as shock and vibration to ensure launch survival.
benefits: This project creates a low-cost flight-ready XRF spectrometer that would benefit Moon Base and Artemis engineering and science goals. XRF enables dust quantification on EVA suits and tools, providing necessary information to mitigate damaging effects. XRF also provides quantitative geochemistry (elemental abundances) useful in identifying resources on the lunar surface and classifying scientific samples of interest for return to Earth.

title: Field Testing of Wind and Weather Lidar for Mars Exploration and Atmospheric Science
lead_organization: Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) — Greenbelt, Maryland
description: We have developed two atmospheric lidar approaches for Mars, both of which are currently TRL 3 to 4. The first is a wind lidar (Mini-MARLI) for Mars orbit which will make wind profile measurements of Mars from the surface to 50 km altitude for the entire globe. The other is surface-based lidar (the Laser Atmospheric Profiling System, LAPS) which will measure real-time vertical profiles of winds, water vapor, dust, and aerosols from the surface to 30 km from a stationary lander. Both instruments are targeted for infusion into the Moon to Mars program and support weather monitoring and forecasting for Mars. In FY27 we propose to combine these two hardware assemblies and perform field experiments at GSFC to demonstrate the ability to measure aerosol backscatter, winds, and water vapor profiles. These experiments will be crucial for obtaining system-level data and informing instrument performance models and engineering trades.
benefits: Combined field experiments at GSFC demonstrating aerosol backscatter, wind, and water vapor profiling; system-level data informing instrument performance models and engineering trades; Mini-MARLI and LAPS advanced from TRL 3-4 toward flight-readiness.

title: Granular Regolith Induced Tribology (GRIT)
lead_organization: Ames Research Center (ARC) — Moffett Field, California
description: Lunar regolith poses a significant and persistent threat to the reliability of mechanical systems required for sustained surface operations. Fine, abrasive dust infiltrates moving components such as bearings, accelerating wear and degrading performance. Despite decades of mitigation research, no established methodology exists to detect regolith-induced degradation from operational data before functional failure occurs. This gap leaves long-duration lunar architectures dependent on conservative scheduled maintenance or reactive failure response, neither well-suited to crewed sorties far from base infrastructure. This proposal seeks to establish a foundation for health management of regolith-exposed mechanical systems. We will develop a repeatable experimental framework that couples controlled regolith simulant exposure with synchronized multimodal data acquisition on a representative rolling-element bearing assembly, capturing the progression of damage rather than a single failure endpoint. A deliberately broad sensor suite — vibration, motor current, torque, temperature, and borescope imagery — enables data-driven down select of the modalities and features most diagnostic of regolith-induced wear. Deliverables include a documented test fixture and protocol, a publicly releasable run-to-degradation dataset, and recommendations for sensing strategies in future lunar surface mechanisms. The work directly supports NASA's transition from short-duration sorties to sustained crewed lunar presence
benefits: Develop a repeatable experimental framework that couples controlled regolith simulant exposure with synchronized multimodal data acquisition on a representative rolling-element bearing assembly, capturing the progression of damage rather than a single failure endpoint.

title: ELITES (Engineered Lunar Infrastructure for Thermal and Electrical Sinks) –ISRU Local Heat (thermal) and Electrical charge (dust mitigation) Sinks for Sustainable Lunar Exploration
lead_organization: Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) — Greenbelt, Maryland
description: For Artemis missions, the lack of reliable thermal and electrical grounding on the Moon presents environmental obstacles that threaten mission success and long-duration survival. To achieve sustainable Moon-to-Mars (M2M) exploration, cryogenic thermal management and lunar dust mitigation are top priorities, designated #1 in STMD Shortfalls and M2M Technology Gaps. This IRAD addresses both with a single solution: creating local subsurface heat and electrical charge sinks using Engineered Lunar Regolith Composites (ELCs). Current space radiators demand large surface footprints, impose substantial Earth-to-Moon mass penalties, require view factor controls, lack heat regeneration capabilities, and suffer degradation from dust accumulation. In contrast, conductive heat dissipation into the lunar subsurface by exploiting the natural thermal gradient offers a transformative ISRU alternative. This approach benefits from the abundance of lunar regolith to minimize added mass and mission footprint, while also avoiding potential lunar dust degradation risks. However, native regolith is highly insulating. Goddard’s Cryogenics team recently demonstrated an approach (published in Cryogenics, 2025) integrating lunar simulants with phase change materials and micro/nano carbon-based fillers. Under lunar-simulated conditions, these ELCs showed a >100x enhancement in effective thermal conductivity and thermal inertia, which are two critical parameters to achieve reliable high-performance heat sink systems. Furthermore, utilizing the natural thermal gradient, thermal energy stored in subsurface ELCs could be extracted as electrical energy to power survival mechanisms during the sunless lunar night. Preliminary cryogenic, high-vacuum testing on the same materials architecture without any modification also exhibited enhanced electrical conductivity (with complementary cryogenic temperature-dependent electrical measurements being delivered this summer by two OSTEM interns). This establishes the ELCs’ dual-functional capability: effective conductive heat rejection and simultaneous electrical charge migration. This provides local grounding pathways to mitigate lunar dust and helps discharge electrostatic buildup on spacesuits caused by dust and space charge bombardment, ensuring astronaut safety. Scalable from surface instruments to habitats, this technology transforms the lunar environment into a resource. It directly addresses M2M Gaps (#0801: Lunar Dust Tolerant System and Dust Mitigation; #0301: Systems to Survive and Operate through Extended Periods of Lunar Shadow) and STMD Shortfalls (#1618 [Rank #1]: Survive and operate through the lunar night; #1595: Energy storage for robust operations; #1616: Dissipation of electrical charge; #1047: Active dust mitigation). This IRAD aims to advance the dual-functional ELC system from TRL-3 to TRL-4 through a cross-disciplinary Goddard collaboration (cryogenic/thermal, mechanical, materials, and contamination). The team will optimize filler dispersion, injected form factors, and low-loss materials. At GSFC’s Cryogenic Lunar Environmental Test Lab (B25), the existing apparatus will be modified with spring-enhanced electrical probes. This addresses sample contraction uncertainties, allowing for the reliable measurement of cryogenic temperature-dependent bulk electrical conductivity without significant system design modifications. This IRAD resource will be essential to continuously grow and develop GSFC civil servants’ unique lunar sample characterization expertise, positioning the center as a critical contributor to Artemis (including an ongoing collaborative effort with the JSC Astromaterials team on establishing the lunar icy sample database). Immediate applications include providing thermal balance and temporary electrical grounding for a cryogenic icy lunar sample return dewar to survive in lunar shadows for Goddard's ongoing STACIS (Storage Transport Acquisition of Cryogenic Icy Samples) project targeting Artemis 5/6 launches, as well as for Goddard’s multifunctional nanosensor platform lunar surface instrument package. Within 2-3 years, beyond leveraging our established expertise and facilities, this ready-to-adopt subsystem technology can be integrated into DALI, PICASSO, and PRISM programs, LTVs, CLPS landers, and habitats for lunar infrastructure.
benefits: ELCs advanced from TRL-3 to TRL-4; >100x improvement in thermal conductivity/inertia; dual-function thermal heat rejection and electrical charge dissipation; scalable from instruments to habitats; immediate application to STACIS cryogenic icy sample return dewar for Artemis 5/6.

title: Hypersonic Flight Deflection Measurement System
lead_organization: Armstrong Flight Research Center (AFRC) — Edwards, California
description: Current SoA for deflection measurement in hypersonic vehicles is to infer deflections from temperature data and/or limited point measurements of strain (OGA programs), or from acceleration data (X-51). These methods have significant uncertainty.​ NASA AFRC has extensive history with camera-based flight deflection measurement systems (AAW, HiMAT, YF-12) up to Mach 2.52. This history is not well-understood by current flight programs.​ Packaging improvements and processing improvements in modern electronics will allow a similar architecture to be packaged in a small form factor even when ruggedized for hypersonic flight. Recent aero-optic characterization work performed for hypersonic seeker windows can be leveraged to increase the operating envelope of the architecture​
benefits: This project seeks to perform a laboratory demonstration of a reliable method for making deflection measurements on a hypersonic vehicle, generating data to inform a white paper for advocacy for infusion in NASA and/or DoD flight programs​

title: Investigation of Microwave Photonics for Upper Atmosphere Sounding
lead_organization: Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) — Greenbelt, Maryland
description: The proposed project aims at supporting the technology development of hyperspectral microwave photonic instruments for Earth and planetary upper atmospheric sounding. Upper atmospheric sounding is critical for national security, weather forecasting, and space weather risk modeling. To replace bulky traditional hardware, this proposal introduces a microwave photonics approach using high-speed ADCs for direct optical sampling in the Second Nyquist Zone and polarization decomposition in the optical domain to analyze polarized electromagnetic radiation.
benefits: Technology development for hyperspectral microwave photonic instruments for Earth and planetary upper atmospheric sounding; high-speed ADC direct optical sampling in the Second Nyquist Zone; polarization decomposition in optical domain; compact photonic architecture replacing bulky traditional hardware.

title: Integration of Additive Manufacturing and Ultrasonic Welding for Advanced Manufacturing of Polymers and Composites
lead_organization: Glenn Research Center (GRC) — Cleveland, Ohio
description: To demonstrate combined thermoplastic (TPC) joining and additive manufacturing (AM) to support sustained presence on the moon; addressing challenges in manufacturing, joining, and repair of polymers and composites on the lunar surface
benefits: This proposal aims to leverage established thermoplastic welding processes to complement additive manufacturing and enable in-space (1) joining of AM polymers (2) repair of TPCs and (3) increased interlaminar strength of AM polymers. Demonstration of these manufacturing capabilities improves the state of the art in manufacturing and joining with this class of materials.

title: Quantum Computing Algorithms for NASA Applications
lead_organization: Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) — Greenbelt, Maryland
description: This is a proposal to study future applications of Quantum Computing (QC) to NASA’s strategic mission. While a fully operational quantum computer may still be years away, recent experimental progress has been significant and certainly warrants more attention. To this end, we will develop efficient new QC algorithms for solving coupled partial differential equations, with particular attention to how these tools may be applied to the most challenging NASA computational problems such as numerical relativity, radiation transport, atmospheric chemistry, materials science, finite element models, and simulation of N-body systems.
benefits: Efficient new QC algorithms for coupled PDEs; applications to numerical relativity, radiation transport, atmospheric chemistry, materials science, finite element models, and N-body simulation; positioning NASA for the computational revolution ahead of fully operational quantum computer availability.

title: VAULT: Volatile Autonomous Ultrawide-Band Lunar Tomographer
lead_organization: Ames Research Center (ARC) — Moffett Field, California
description: NASA’s Moon‑to‑Mars objectives require the ability to locate and characterize subsurface volatiles and geotechnical hazards to support a sustainable lunar presence. Current planetary Ground Penetrating Radar systems are limited to monostatic configurations that produce 2D radargrams, constraining science return and autonomous operations. VAULT leverages Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory’s (LLNL) proven Multistatic Imaging Radar capable of delivering real-time, centimeter-scale 3D subsurface imagery down to a 10-meter depth. Recent testbed evaluations by USGS, LLNL, and NASA Ames at the SSERVI lunar regolith facility have already demonstrated the system’s unique capability to resolve frozen volatiles at 5% weight concentrations. In collaboration with LTV providers, USGS, and LLNL, we have identified three key barriers towards advancement to lunar applications: data volumes that exceed lunar downlink capacity, commercial electronics unrated for extreme space environments, and the absence of an integrated flight architecture. VAULT addresses these challenges through a comprehensive mission design with payload accommodation architecture, a spaceflight electronics roadmap, and a closed-loop edge-computing autonomy framework. This autonomy system will process raw tomographic returns in real-time to actively guide rover trajectory decisions under USGS planetary science constraints. The project delivers a flight‑ready mission proposal package and space‑hardening roadmap, positioning Ames to lead future lunar efforts.
benefits: The primary goal of Project VAULT is to develop a validated reference architecture and an intelligent onboard autonomy suite to integrate Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory’s (LLNL) unique multistatic tomographic Ground Penetrating Radar (GPR) onto a baseline Lunar Terrain Vehicle (LTV) chassis under U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) science constraints. Develop add-on sensor reference architecture that provides the high-confidence, 3D volumetric data required to guide tactical rover operations. Rather than "drilling blind" and risking costly, time-consuming drilling or regolith-sampling maneuvers on uncharacterized ground, VAULT provides the detailed, contact-level subsurface mapping needed to de-risk and target sampling sites with high confidence.

title: Fast and Agile Data Assimilation Framework for MLT and VLEO Instrument Development
lead_organization: Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) — Greenbelt, Maryland
description: This proposed effort aims to develop a fast, modularized, and lightweight data assimilation. This project develops a fast, AI-compatible, and modular data assimilation (DA) framework using WACCM-X (the NCAR Whole Atmosphere Community Climate Model with thermosphere and ionosphere eXtension; the core whole atmosphere general circulation model), ARTS (Atmospheric Radiative Transfer Simulator; the radiative transfer module), and NEDAS (Next-generation Ensemble Data Assimilation System; the DA module) to support mission and instrument development in the Mesosphere and Lower Thermosphere (MLT) and Very Low Earth Orbit (VLEO) environments. Bypassing the inflexible, slowly developing legacy systems that target at operational use, this innovation enables rapid impact assessment of new instruments. The capability directly targets infusion into Terrestrial Resource and Hazard Prediction (TRaHP) operational systems, supporting NASA’s Moon-to-Mars launch/re-entry needs and the accelerated delivery of high-priority space weather data for commercial and national security space operations. (DA) framework specifically designed to support mission and instrument development for the Mesosphere and Lower Thermosphere (MLT, 60-200 km) and Very Low Earth Orbit (VLEO, 200-400 km) environments. Current NASA legacy DA systems are computationally inflexible for evaluating new MLT instrument designs and lack AI compatibility. To overcome these bottlenecks, this project will integrate an agile and AI-friendly suite of open-source modules to enable quick impact assessment cycle of heliosphere weather forecast which will be directly tied to instrument parameters so to effectively speed-up the instrument development cycle. Building on an offline framework initiated under an FY26 IRAD, this project will develop a fully functional online DA framework and demonstrate its capabilities through two use cases: EZIE/THz instrument data assimilation and GNSS-POD derived mass density assimilation. Furthermore, the team will develop a digital-twin data assimilation component to prove the framework's AI compatibility. By creating this highly versatile ecosystem, the project directly supports the Terrestrial Resource and Hazard Prediction (TRaHP) SFA's strategic goal of eroding the artificial boundary between terrestrial Earth Science and Heliophysics space weather. Ultimately, this innovation will enable the rapid prototyping of orbital assets, provide accurate near-real-time environmental forecasts, and ensure Goddard maintains technical leadership as NASA and commercial sectors rapidly expand operations into VLEO.
benefits: Fully functional online DA framework integrating WACCM-X, ARTS, and NEDAS; two demonstrated use cases (EZIE/THz instrument DA; GNSS-POD mass density assimilation); digital-twin DA component for AI compatibility; rapid impact assessment of new MLT instruments.

title: Capillary Absorption Spectroscopy for Exploration and Science (CAS)
lead_organization: Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) — Greenbelt, Maryland
description: Our Capillary Absorption Spectrometer (CAS) is a mid-infrared tunable laser spectrometer that identifies molecular species and isotopologues through their unique absorption signatures in the 2–16 µm "molecular fingerprint" region. This technology has been developed under SBIR and DALI funding by Optoknowledge Systems, Inc. (OKSI) partnering with Dr. Jen Stern at GSFC. A prototype CAS instrument built under the Phase II SBIR will be delivered to Dr. Stern’s laboratory in Summer 2026. To infuse this into upcoming GSFC mission concepts, it is necessary to 1) evaluate CAS performance on relevant sample gas mixtures and 2) develop a GSFC sample handling system compatible with in situ measurements as well as returned samples.
benefits: CAS instrument performance evaluation on relevant sample gas mixtures; development of GSFC sample handling system compatible with in situ measurements and returned samples; mid-IR molecular fingerprint region (2–16 µm) species and isotopologue identification.

title: Investigating COTS magnetometers for spaceflight research applications
lead_organization: Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) — Greenbelt, Maryland
description: This work assesses the viability of modifying commercial magnetometer sensor technology in order to produce space flight instruments capable of observations required for science and operations but using less resources than typical for science-grade magnetometers. The proposed work would leverage the unique capabilities of Goddard’s world-class expertise in magnetometry and the Mario H. Acuña Magnetic Testing Facility to perform comprehensive, in-depth characterization and performance evaluation of three magnetometers: a magneto-inductive magnetometer, a miniaturized fluxgate magnetometer, and an optically pumped quantum magnetometer. The resulting insights will enable our team to implement design improvements to ultimately produce magnetometers optimized for low size, weight, and power requirements (SWaP) that can satisfy the performance requirements for some terrestrial and heliophysics missions, including missions specifically tailored to low-resource space weather monitoring and characterization.
benefits: Comprehensive characterization of three magnetometer types (magneto-inductive, miniaturized fluxgate, optically pumped quantum) at GSFC's Mario H. Acuña Magnetic Testing Facility; design improvements producing low-SWaP magnetometers satisfying performance requirements for terrestrial and heliophysics missions.

title: GN&C Modeling, Simulation, and Integration of ANTS
lead_organization: Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) — Huntsville, Alabama
description: This proposal is one piece in the future development path of Autonomous Network of Teleoperated Systems (ANTS), leveraging assets and expertise from Mission and Fault Management, GN&C, and Human Factors. ANTS closes a critical gap in the interoperability of lunar mobile assets, serving as an “air traffic controller” for multiple heterogenous systems. ANTS-type infrastructure will be necessary if there are two or more lunar assets operating in the same area. The long-term goal is to stand up a high-fidelity simulation in Human Factors' lunar lighting and terrain simulation, LEVR (Lunar Environments in Virtual Reality), utilizing GN&C-generated physics-based rover models, to develop, test, and verify Mission and Fault Management’s ANTS capabilities with multiple rovers in a highly realistic lunar environment. Although this proposal focuses on the GN&C component of the technology maturation path, great care has been taken to ensure extensibility and sustainability for future funding efforts. ROS was selected as the common framework to define the interfaces between all three aspects. This proposal seeks to implement these interfaces and complete the GN&C elements, with support from Mission and Fault Management on critical ANTS updates. GN&C will be responsible for the development of physics-based and kinematically-consistent rover models in an industry-standard GN&C development tool, Simulink. Although a current implementation of ANTS exists within Simulink, rover models are simple and used exclusively for debugging purposes rather than physically-realistic simulations, including holonomic motion, electric motor torque and speed limits, and wheel-slippage. GN&C will implement generalized and extensible rover models in a “crawl, walk, run” fashion, starting with a simple unicycle model, followed by differential drive, followed by steering linkage models. These standardized models are representative and extensible to current and future lunar rover concepts and can be tailored to each mission. GN&C and Mission and Fault Management will implement a ROS wrapper around these models to allow the easy portability of models to other assets, including Human Factors’ LEVR. Mission and Fault Management will assess ANTS performance under several rover models.
benefits: The expected outcome of this study is a maturation of the ANTS technology with physics-based rover models, enabling high quality simulations for a variety of mobile lunar assets. Goals: 1. Integrate Robot Operating System (ROS) framework message passing interface, positioning this work to be readily accessible for future development. 2. Further the capability of Autonomous Network of Teleoperated Systems (ANTS) by increasing the number of rovers that can be commanded in simulation. 3. Increase fidelity of current ANTS rover models in Simulink to use physics-based and kinematically-consistent equations of motion.

title: SLABs (Solar Light Absorbing Bricks derived from regolith composites)
lead_organization: Kennedy Space Center (KSC) — Kennedy Space Center, Florida
description: The lunar surface ranges from -250C to 121C. Adequate thermal regulation during the lunar night is necessary for projects to operate. Thermal Wadis are highly conductive regolith-based thermal masses that are capable of redistributing heat to surrounding systems. By leveraging the composite 3D printing technology achieved by ACTSE (Advanced Compounding Twin Screw Extruder), a thermal wadi pad composite will be extruded, and demonstrate a material that requires low energy to construct and utilize existing additive construction and TVAC capabilities . Its thermal storage capabilities will be tested during a 14-day period (a lunar night).
benefits: A method to develop structures with built in thermal control from lunar regolith with minimal terrestrial material. Modular versions of SLAB technology could be placed by electronic components and provide heat for robotic exploration systems during their mission. This technology would not just be limited to solar for heat input but could also feed on excess heat from other systems, such as batteries, to store and redistribute heat during the lunar night. In essence, this project would result in a natural heat sink, heat source, and structural component all in one material. This would be ideal for future moon base missions, as it would enable equipment with the ability to survive in long-term cryogenic conditions.

title: A photonic-lantern-based hybrid receiver to advance a Martian atmospheric CO₂ flux profiling lidar
lead_organization: Langley Research Center (LaRC) — Hampton, Virginia
description: The proposed efforts enable us to demonstrate a Photonic-Lantern (PL)-based Hybrid Lidar Receiver (HLR), as shown in Figure, at 2.0 µm for a Martian atmospheric CO₂ Flux Profiling Lidar (FPL) for simultaneous profiling of the CO₂ density and 4D-wind in the Martian atmosphere to retrieve CO₂ flux and characterize CO₂ cycles in real time for future Mars missions, including safe Entry, Descent, and Landing (EDL) on Mars. There is currently no lidar capable of profiling at a single wavelength. Developing a Hybrid Lidar Receiver (HLR) that enables profiling is therefore a critical technology gap.
benefits: Integration and demonstration of the photonic‑lantern based HLR will establish the first functional building block for a Martian atmospheric CO₂ FPL. Confirmation of the technical feasibility of combining CO₂ DIAL and 4D‑wind measurements enables future CO₂ flux retrievals and dynamic CO₂ cycles

title: Metamaterials Replacing Beryllium using Architected Materials
lead_organization: Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) — Greenbelt, Maryland
description: Beryllium (Be) substrates enable lightweight, dimensionally stable optics for spaceborne lidar telescopes, however, impose long lead times, high cost, and supply risk. This IRAD proposes to mature and scale an additively manufactured (AM) metamaterials substrate that delivers Be-like thermomechanical performance for meter-class lidar telescope optics using readily available alloys. Building on a recent Journal from Imaging Science & Technology (JIST) by Souk et al., 2026, which demonstrated a scalable metamaterial architecture using Al6061 RAM2. This metamaterial design process achieving within 2 µm surface deformation of a Be I 220H control with only 10% mass increase and at >90% reductions in cost and lead time. Our team suggests extending the design, manufacturing, and verification approach to telescope-relevant scales and environments.
benefits: Scale AM Al6061 RAM2 metamaterial substrate to telescope-relevant scales; within 2 µm surface deformation matching Be I-220H control; >90% reduction in cost and lead time; only 10% mass increase vs. beryllium; eliminates supply chain risk for meter-class lidar telescope optics.

title: Construction Implements for ISRU Construction (ConstructIICons)
lead_organization: Kennedy Space Center (KSC) — Kennedy Space Center, Florida
description: Further KSC’s extraterrestrial compaction for ISRU construction capabilities that meet potential partner needs and expands applicability to multiple programs with a focus on Moon Base needs. Project focuses on advancing the MEERCAT (Multifunctional End Effector for Regolith Construction, Acquisition, and Transfer) compactor and construction demonstrator, and STOMP (Site Preparation Tooling for Operations on Mobility Platforms ) a large-scale roller compactor for foundations, roadways, and landing pad construction. Combined, these technologies present a pathways from early technology demonstrations of compaction up to full-scale construction and geotechnical quality control measurements.
benefits: Further study and demonstration of MEERCAT geotechnical and compaction quality control capabilities, integrating the existing STOMP roller compactor on RASSOR 2 for robotic demonstration, and design of a TRL 5 STOMP (design only)

title: Lunar Water Mapper
lead_organization: Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) — Greenbelt, Maryland
description: Lunar Water Mapper (LuWaM) is a low-cost CubeSat lunar orbiter for remote-sensing water ice deposits on the Moon, where the operating wavelength (I=6.12mm) is the H2O bending absorption line which is not shared by OH-bearing materials. The field illuminated by a compact mid-Infrared Quantum cascade laser (MI-QCL) will be imaged on a Mercury Cadmium Telluride (HgCdTe) photodiode array through a compact telescope. Our success will support the In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU) and future Artemis programs.
benefits: Low-cost CubeSat lunar orbiter for remote sensing of water ice deposits; operates at H₂O bending absorption line (not shared by OH-bearing materials) using mid-IR QCL and HgCdTe photodiode array; supports ISRU water ice resource identification.

title: JOEEE: Jumping Orientable Extreme Environment Explorer
lead_organization: Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) — Greenbelt, Maryland
description: We propose modifying and augmenting the JOEEE hopping and cartwheeling mobility system with a multi-function tether to enable mobility into and long duration operations within a Lunar PSR. The Jumping Orientable Extreme Environment Explorer (JOEEE) is a novel surface mobility platform that enables mission concepts such as exploring craters, Lunar PSRs, Lunar lava tubes, extreme low gravity bodies (comets and asteroids), and interaction with astronauts (is safe to handle). The unique maneuvering capability provided by internal brake-able flywheels in JOEEE facilitates mobility of imagers, spectrometers, magnetometers, and other instruments over and into terrain inaccessible to wheeled/tracked rovers or rocket propelled hoppers while the low cost/complexity of the system enables single or multi-robot mission concepts. The goals of this follow on Early Stage Innovation project are to mature TRL of JOEEE from numerical simulation to laboratory demonstrations, perform life testing of critical mechanisms, and continue to meet with instrument developers to target PRISM, CLPS, Ignition, Artemis, and DALI.
benefits: Modification of JOEEE hopping/cartwheeling mobility system with multi-function tether for Lunar PSR entry and long-duration operations; maturation from numerical simulation to laboratory demonstrations; life testing of critical mechanisms; single and multi-robot mission concept enablement.

title: High-Temp EFPI Accelerometer Technology
lead_organization: Armstrong Flight Research Center (AFRC) — Edwards, California
description: EFPI based sensor for accelerometer that can withstand temperatures up to ~1800°F​ Replacing tiny fiber reflector end with reflective metallic diving board deflector ​ Can reach temperatures up to 1800 °F degrees, limits of gold coating on EFPI fiber, different coated fibers currently under research for survivability far beyond 1800°F​ Immune to EMI and thermal effects (plasma) experienced during hypersonic flight​ Can be plugged into and interrogated via pre-existing WDM flight rated and proven systems​
benefits: Measure dynamic accelerations at extreme temperatures (~1800 F) during ground and/or high speed flight (hypersonic)​

title: Charging at the Moon: Impact Assessment
lead_organization: Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) — Greenbelt, Maryland
description: We propose the formal onboarding and operational integration of the Stubbs et al. (2014) lunar surface charging model at CCMC. This initiative encompasses two tightly coupled objectives: Run-on-Request Research Tool: Deploy the model on CCMC's platform for community use — enabling scientists, mission designers, and commercial operators to simulate surface charging under user-specified conditions. Real-Time Operational Diagnostic: Drive the model with live solar wind inputs (DSCOVR/SOLAR-1/ACE) for continuous surface potential estimates at the Moon. When the Moon transits Earth's magnetotail (~4 days each month), direct solar wind measurements are unavailable; in this regime, high-resolution global MHD model outputs hosted at CCMC will serve as plasma environment inputs, ensuring uninterrupted operational coverage. Once validated, the tool integrates into M2M SWAO real-time toolboxes. This is a prime R2O2R investment: transitioning a peer-reviewed model into an operational crew and space hardware safety asset.
benefits: Operational lunar surface charging model integrated at CCMC for community use; real-time surface potential estimates driven by live solar wind inputs (DSCOVR/ACE); uninterrupted coverage during magnetotail transits; integration into M2M SWAO real-time toolboxes.

title: Advancing Core Hyperspectral and Ultraviolet Imaging Technologies Through Focal Plane Array Implementation on Digital Read Out Integrated Circuits
lead_organization: Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) — Greenbelt, Maryland
description: Goddard spaceflight center has made considerable progress advancing hyperspectral imaging focal planes and deep-ultraviolet (DUV) detectors including quantum dot (QD) based hyperspectral imagers which are beginning to enable spectrometer-on-a-chip implementations and silicon carbide (SiC) focal plane arrays which demonstrate solar blind UV detection combined with femtoamp level dark current and radiation hardness. However, both of these technologies are at this point limited by their readout integrate circuitry (ROIC) with QD filter array’s performance limited by their underlying detector and SiC arrays confined to 1D configurations. We propose the transition of QD hyperspectral imagers and SiC based UV focal plane arrays to emerging, 2D, digital ROICs (DROICs) to improve performance and simplify operation by spinning up a camera development platform built around Attollo Engineering’s AE1702 VGA DROIC, demonstrating direct signal readout from QD active materials, a fundamental advancement is in the operation of QD detectors, and, as a stretch goal, performing an integration of a small scale 2D SiC arrays to demonstrate 2D UV imaging. Both technologies have broad applications commensurate with “coupling of terrestrial and space weather to fully unify the Earth system from below the surface to the edge of space” highly relevant to TRaHP and the transition to DROICs is a critical step in this path to accelerate the development of these cutting edge technologies in preparation for spaceflight deployments.
benefits: Transition of QD hyperspectral imagers and SiC-based UV focal plane arrays to 2D DROICs; improved performance and simplified operation; demonstration of direct signal readout from QD active materials; 2D SiC UV imaging demonstration; accelerated development of cutting-edge imaging technologies for spaceflight.

title: Computationally Designed Protein Sensors for Assessing Lunar Dust Impact on Human Organoid Models
lead_organization: Ames Research Center (ARC) — Moffett Field, California
description: Spaceflight induces a variety of unique stressors on the human body, including microgravity, radiation, and, if exploring the Moon, lunar dust. Organoids are ideal systems to test how humans will respond to these stressors. However, traditional analysis technologies for monitoring health markers in organoids do not meet the mass and volume restrictions for launch. Although lightweight monitoring platforms have been developed at NASA ARC, their reliance on commercially available antibodies limits their sensitivity, shelf life, and applicability to new biomarkers. Here, we propose to use computational modeling to enhance the sensitivity, shelf life, and applicability of existing biosensor platforms. Using a combination of machine learning and physics-based modeling, we will create a design pipeline that results in novel protein sequences to detect a given biomarker target. We will use this pipeline to create a sensor to detect mucus in lung organoids, an important biological response to lunar dust. Finally, we will apply our new sensor to detect lung organoid mucus levels based as a function of simulated lunar dust exposure. Our new technology will enhance the sensitivity and shelf life of the current state-of-the-art in detecting organoid response to simulated lunar dust, while enabling rapid application to other biomarkers.
benefits: Using a combination of machine learning and physics-based modeling, we will create a design pipeline that results in novel protein sequences to detect a given biomarker target. We will use this pipeline to create a sensor to detect mucus in lung organoids, an important biological response to lunar dust. Finally, we will apply our new sensor to detect lung organoid mucus levels based as a function of simulated lunar dust exposure. Our new technology will enhance the sensitivity and shelf life of the current state-of-the-art in detecting organoid response to simulated lunar dust, while enabling rapid application to other biomarkers.

title: Cross Layer Spectrum Aware Cognitive Control Plane and Intelligent Routing Engine (CLAIRE)
lead_organization: A10 Systems Inc. d/b/a AiRANACULUS — Massachusetts
description: AiRANACULUS and partners proposes an innovative Cross Layer Spectrum Aware Cognitive Control Plane and Intelligent Routing Engine (CLAIRE) solution to increase mission science data return, improve resource efficiencies for NASA missions and communication networks and ensure resilience in the unpredictable space environment. An Autonomous Intelligent Reconfiguration system is envisioned to sense, detect, adapt, and learn from its experiences and environment to optimize the communications capabilities for the lunar surface, lunar proximity and cislunar network infrastructure. The NASA CLAIRE CCRPP project will enhance the TRL (5 to 7) and MRL (4 to 6) of the technologies developed through NASA CLAIRE project (Contract #80NSSC21C0510 same name adopted) which completed Phase II and Phase II-E. The CCRPP will also leverage the work been carried out on NASA INSPiRE Project (Contract # 80NSSC22CA141) where Phase II has been completed and Phase II-E is on-going. CLAIRE provides wide-band Radio Frequency (RF) sensing, cognitive control plane as an APP, interference mitigation techniques, autonomous channel assignments and congestion aware packet forwarding. INSPiRE builds on CLAIRE and provides spectrum and interference aware routing, network slicing over heterogeneous multivendor network to maintain Quality of Service (QoS), policy-based prioritization and INSPiRE enhanced HDTN Contact Graph Routing (CGR). CLAIRE engages in local link level optimization, INSPiRE engages in global optimization of the network for a wide variety of users. In this project, CLAIRE and INSPiRE will interface with the Glenn Research Center (GRC) Cognitive Engine (CE). CLAIRE and INSPiRE functionality will be integrated into TES CubeSat, and flight tested. CLAIRE and INSPiRE will be integrated into Nokia Banshee Mobile Radio (BMR) and 5G O-RAN platform provided by Nvidia / Radisys / Juniper. Together, this will demonstrate resilient wireless operation on lunar surface and lunar proximity networks.
benefits: CLAIRE and INSPiRE provide following Capabilities and Applications: • CLAIRE APP enabled Cognitive Control Plane provides spectrum and network situational awareness. Application Layer Heartbeat (HTBT) messages may be sent over any IP-enabled network. This enables Link Optimization using Dynamic Spectrum Access / Dynamic Channel Assignment and Dynamic Bandwidth Adaptation. • Wide-Band RF Sensing with Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning enables detection and characterization of interference with >90% Probability of Correct Classification of Interference with 90% throughput improvement in presence of interference – CLAIRE and INSPiRE provide Interference Mitigation and Congestion Control techniques such as Dynamic Spectrum Access (DSA), Interference and Congestion Aware Packet Forwarding (IAPF), Spectrum and Interference Aware Routing (SIAR). • INSPiRE enhanced HDTN Contact Graph Routing - CLAIRE and INSPiRE provide DTN access to a comprehensive global network context, making possible the identification of optimized transmissions for bundles. This leads to enhanced Contact Graph Routing (CGR) enabling routing optimization by selecting outducts for bundle transmissions. • CLAIRE and INSPiRE provide Spectrum and Network Situational Awareness – Enables NASA to autonomously find and fix the root cause of service quality degradation. • Network Slicing over heterogeneous multi-vendor network to maintain QoS – provides 10x improvement in communications quality in presence of interference and congestion. • INSPiRE / CLAIRE enhance COTS 4G/5G and NTN - NASA can leverage commercial open solutions that can scale. AiRANACULUS' motto is Intelligent RF and Networking from Space to Smart Cities. Our mission is to make ALL radios robust and resilient to interference and congestion using advanced signal processing and machine learning-based solutions. Our CLAIRE and INSPiRE technologies offer scalable solutions for Next-Gen Communications, Radar, Electronic Warfare, and SIGINT applications. These technologies apply across commercial terrestrial (3G/4G/5G/Wi-Fi), space (LEO/MEO/GEO/Relays/Gateways), and backhaul (Optical Fiber/Coax) networks, with built-in security and privacy, making them ideal for DoD, DHS, NSA, FAA, and other federal agencies. Key Applications of CLAIRE and INSPiRE: 1. Advanced Communications (5G/6G): o Enhances interference and congestion tolerance for future 5G/6G networks. o Addresses the private 5G market, projected to reach $665B by 2028. o Collaboration with the Army on next-gen anti-jam systems. 2. Command and Control (C2) Constructs: o Empowers SATCOM, military, and cellular radios with cognitive capabilities via RF and cross-layer sensing. o Supports Joint All Domain C2 (JADC2) and ABMS by enabling technology-agnostic control. o Ensures critical data delivery with network slicing for heterogeneous networks. 3. Wideband Sensing & Interference Management: o Telecom operators spend $600M annually on interference detection; our solutions accelerate detection and localization. o AiRANACULUS contributes to Intelligence Community programs for RF anomaly detection. 4. Space Applications (LEO/MEO/GEO): o Addresses interference challenges between terrestrial and non-terrestrial networks. o Developed a multi-channel wide-band receiver for NASA’s Artemis Moon Mission and LunaNet, ensuring high-throughput, interference-free communications. Our technology is poised to revolutionize both commercial and defense communication landscapes, ensuring seamless connectivity and resilient operations.

title: Manufacturing Radiation Tolerant Silicon Carbide Switches
lead_organization: CoolCAD Electronics, LLC — College Park, Maryland
description: The goal of this program is to streamline the manufacturing of radiation tolerant high voltage silicon carbide power MOSFETs in the US, and therefore to build a domestic supply chain. High power nuclear electric propulsion, and power processing for the implementation of the Moon vicinity/surface mission require high voltage and power semiconductor switches. To increase efficiency, and to decrease volume and weight of power systems, high voltage-based power distribution and processing networks are critically needed. MOSFETs play a crucial role for power systems typically used in the high voltage, power and frequency range. Additionally, silicon carbide (SiC) MOSFETs provide advantages over their silicon (Si) and gallium nitride (GaN) alternatives in the voltage range of interest. Silicon carbide is the most mature among the wide bandgap semiconductors in terms of fabrication and processing, offering the most direct path to radiation tolerance, as well as electrical performance. Commercial SiC power devices are tolerant of ionizing dose and displacement damage, but they suffer from single event effects. During our Phase II, we work on novel designs and process engineering methods to design more radiation tolerant silicon carbide power devices. The experiments show that we indeed achieved radiation tolerance and performance. This sequential work uses this foundation to make these radhard power devices and aims to build a long-term source for these devices employing domestic foundries. This requires creation of the supply chain for the low volume manufacture of these devices in the US for sensitive and critical applications. This also requires building the capability of mass manufacture of these devices domestically for NASA, DoD and commercial uses. To this end, we will work with two US foundries that serve critical-need as well as commercial markets.
benefits: To address the need for high voltage radiation tolerant power devices for the future lunar microgrid, for other deep space exploration missions and bases, and for space nuclear electric propulsion, we design and fabricate radiation-tolerant high voltage silicon carbide power devices. Electric propulsion and power processing are identified as some of the critical technologies to be addressed as part of the global exploration roadmap for the implementation of the near-future Moon vicinity/surface mission. In addition, solar and nuclear electric propulsion, and extreme environment avionics with high overall shortfall ranks require high power and/or voltage circuits. The proposed work relates to five among the top fifteen shortfalls in the integrated list for civil space shortfall rankings, as written below: #2 1596: High Power Energy Generation on Moon and Mars Surfaces #6 1552: Extreme Environment Avionics #8 709: Nuclear Electric Propulsion for Human Exploration #12 1591: Power Management Systems for Long Duration Lunar and Martian Missions #13 702: Nuclear Thermal Propulsion for Human Exploration Our high voltage and current silicon carbide power transistor technology is to support NASA’s Moon to Mars goals and the Nuclear Electric Propulsion (NEP) Project’s needs for high voltage, high power transistors and diodes, as these are scaled up to megawatt power levels. Additionally, successful demonstration of this technology should enable infusion into the Radioisotope Power Systems (RPS) Program’s power processing systems and Fission Surface Power Project. We will also make high voltage but not high current versions of these devices as well. High voltage circuit applications include voltage sources for multichannel plates (MCPs) that are used in many types of analytical equipment. Of particular interest is particle detection and specifically advancing electrical circuits for electrostatic analyzers for advanced particle detection with smaller footprint instruments. CoolCAD is transitioning its wide bandgap power electronics from prototype to product lines. We envision a dual-use technology where standard devices for renewable energy, and industrial or power conversion circuit applications will lead the demand in making these silicon carbide power devices. In parallel, we will make radiation tolerant power MOSFETs that take advantage of the volume production related to these other widespread terrestrial-use products. Renewable energy has increased considerably since the turn of the century, driven largely by solar power. According to the US Department of Energy, the total capacity of solar power installed in residential and commercial applications has increased by more than 500% from that time. By leveraging the inherent flexibility of solar photovoltaics (PV), energy storage system (ESS), and the electric vehicle (EV) charging technology, the integrated systems can reduce the total capital and operational costs of these distributed energy resource (DER) assets. Uses of wide bandgap semiconductor-based power devices and next-generation silicon carbide (SiC) power devices would result in higher efficiencies in charging, solar and power conversion systems, decreasing the time for the system to pay itself off through savings. Furthermore, wide bandgap semiconductor devices can be operated at relatively high frequencies, enabling use of smaller passives. This would decrease the overall size of any DC power conversion circuit. Besides real estate savings and potentially denser installations, this would add less complexity and cost to wiring and installation. Besides standard use power devices, the radiation tolerant devices we manufacture can be used in satellites and near nuclear reactors. Of particular interest is the combined tolerance to radiation and temperature. In the case of hypersonics, not only radiation tolerance is required but also temperature hardened electronics are needed.

title: Radiation Hardened Power Efficient Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Processor (AIML)
lead_organization: CFD Research Corporation — Huntsville, Alabama
description: Radiation Hardened Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning (AIML) processors are essential to NASA applications due to unavoidable evolution in technology that brings computational complexity. Traditional radiation hardening methods incur high size, weight, and power (SWaP) cost. We propose a radiation hardening scheme that employs intelligent analysis of vulnerabilities in the AIML processor that enables hybrid selective redundancy implementation to allow self-healing from radiation effects. The proposed radiation analysis method will use statistical and probabilistic models that can capture the stochasticity of AI, ML and Neural net inference. In Phase I, we designed and validated the radiation analysis model to study the vulnerabilities in a generic AIML circuit-under-test (CUT). This was followed by design and validation of selective redundancy based radiation hardening scheme for AIML CUT. In Phase II, we will optimize the design to meet NASA requirements, build a prototype, and experimentally verify the performance of radiation hardened AIML processor.
benefits: We anticipate a wide variety of NASA applications and customers for the Radiation Hardened AIML Processor including: (i) R&D of space technologies for use in more demanding NASA applications, (ii) qualification of AIML processors for performance and reliability, (iii) design of AIML processors for use in harsh environments such as space, nuclear radiation environments, etc., and (iv) design of NASA systems and integration of different sub-systems while ensuring performance and reliability. Commercial customers include developers of micro/nano-satellites, avionics, automotive, telecommunication, consumer electronics, industrial data processing and NASA primes developing electronics for commercial space applications.

title: Collaborative Robot Enabled Active Microwave Thermography Nondestructive Evaluation Prototype
lead_organization: Texas Research Institute Austin, Inc. — Austin, Texas
description: Inspection systems are required to safely manufacture components in space, including regolith-based components. NASA is preparing for the next phase of human deep spaceflight which requires much of the materials, structures, and subsystems to be built/assembled in space.
