Shielding allows spacecraft designers to consolidate heat rejection systems placing the greatest burden on more efficient systems. Additionally, nested tanks have to potential to greatly improve packing efficiency compared to equivalent volume but separate tanks.

title: Behavior of Ullage Bubbles during Blowdown in Low-g Experiment​ (BUBBLE)
lead_organization: Glenn Research Center (GRC) — Cleveland, Ohio
description: This activity will design, build, and operate a drop tower test article to provide model validation data for cryogenic tank venting operations in reduced gravity. Objectives of this activity include: Develop a liquid nitrogen drop tower test rig to investigate cryogenic liquid level rise due to bubble displacement while venting a tank. Obtain high-fidelity visualization data of the vapor generation phenomena and measure liquid level rise and tank thermodynamics for robust model validation. Characterize differences in the fundamental physical phenomena between ground and drop tower testing. Characterize liquid level rise as it relates to fill level, vent mass flow rate, and gravity level.
benefits: This activity will address a gap by obtaining reduced gravity cryogenic tank venting data for model validation. Validated models can be used to reduce risk and increase efficiency of tank venting and settling operations for on-orbit cryogenic propellant depots in support of NASA’s future missions.

title: Optical Fiber-based Coriolis Flowmeter (OFCF)
lead_organization: Armstrong Flight Research Center (AFRC) — Edwards, California
description: It is imperative to have an accurate, reliable method to measure cryogenic fluid transfer for in-space and on-surface application. This problem has been continuously been ranked highly under NASA STMD’s shortfall. It is well known that Coriolis-based flowmeter is the most accurate mass-flowmeter, but with drawback being needing heavy and bulky stainless steel enclosure for EMI shielding due to it relied on magnetic sensing. Optical fiber-based Coriolis Flowmeter (OFCF) technology explores using fiber optics sensors to replace the magnetic sensors, therefore eliminating the need of EMI shielding.
benefits: By using optical fiber-based sensors instead of magnetic sensors, EMI shielding from traditional Coriolis flowmeter could be eliminate, which helps reaching the low SWaP (size weight and power) requirement for in-space and on-surface deployment application.

title: Pharmacy Shelf-Life
lead_organization: Johnson Space Center (JSC) — Houston, Texas
description: Exploration missions beyond low Earth orbit will experience significant challenges in crew medical care. Among these challenges are limited or no resupply missions to replenish medication inventory. Ensuring medication safety and efficacy will buy down medical risk. For anticipated medications planned for inclusion in future exploration medical systems, the time from packaging to use will exceed manufacturer-reported shelf-life. This poses a risk that medications may be ineffective when used. This project effort included a literature review, development of a concept of operations for a Mars formulary, a plan for ground and/or flight testing, and investigation into current shelf-life extension of medications of interest.
benefits: The outcome of the pharmacy shelf-life effort will inform medical system contents and packaging techniques. Ensuring medication efficacy beyond expiration dates and shielding technologies will buy down medical risk for future exploration missions. This work will enable safe and effective selection of medications for operational infusion in long duration Artemis and Mars missions.

title: Active Vibration Isolation and Stabilization System (AVISS)
lead_organization: Johnson Space Center (JSC) — Houston, Texas
description: Exercise Countermeasure Systems (CMS) are critical to maintaining crew health while exposed to microgravity. A Vibration Isolation and Stabilization (VIS) system is required to isolate the loads generated during exercise from the vehicle structure, and to provide a stable base for the crewmember to exercise safely. The CMS Exercise hardware on ISS all use passive VIS systems, due to the availability of the mass and volume that these designs require. However, some of these designs require upwards of 1000lbs countermass and are specific to the exercise hardware and modalities it provides, and location in the spacecraft. Future exploration vehicles are expected to be more constrained on available mass and volume, requiring a more compact VIS design. Both Johnson Space Center (JSC) and Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) submitted proposals for an Active VIS in response to the Mars Campaign Office (MCO) FY27 New Start call for proposals. Based on specific expertise from both proposing organizations, MCO has directed that the teams collaborate on the project. In FY25, using discretional funds from JSC/ER (Software, Robotics, and Simulation Division), the JSC team out of ER7 (Simulation and Graphics Branch) evaluated 5 initial Active VIS concepts, before narrowing it down to two: the fixed-base and free-base concepts. At the end of FY25, the team recommended focusing on the fixed-base concept. This concept is different than the existing passive VIS systems that are free-base. As this New Start project kicked off in FY26, with that knowledge in hand, the team comprised of both JSC and JPL personnel agreed to focus on the fixed-base concept design, and identified two approaches for the 6 Degree of Freedom (6DOF) design: Stewart Platform (hexapod) and TRI-DAX (6 individual linear actuators and throwmasses). This project will first work the tasks needed to get to a single recommended AVIS design, and then start building hardware.
benefits: The project seeks to combine JSC’s expertise in exercise system development and corresponding analysis, with JPL’s expertise in precision active isolation system design to develop an Active VIS that helps close ESDMD Technology Gap #0401 with demonstrated performance. Specifically, this effort seeks to provide mass and volume savings on exploration vehicles.

title: Complex Dielectric Characterization and Forward Modeling of Lunar and Martian Materials for Artemis IV LDA and Mars Resource Reconnaissance
lead_organization: Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) — Greenbelt, Maryland
description: This requested short-duration task will complete essential modeling and calibration tasks supporting Agency‑level Moon‑to‑Mars priorities by finalizing complex dielectric permittivity and magnetic permeability analyses of key lunar (NWA 8687) and martian (NWA 16272) samples at 1 GHz using HFSS and previously acquired S‑parameter measurements. The effort will generate validated 3D dielectric tensor models across multiple sample orientations, enabling direct scientific connection to current RIMFAX GPR observations in Jezero Crater and future measurements from the Artemis IV “LDA” landed experiment. Deliverables include forward‑modeled dielectric properties, a near‑final research article for AAS/PSJ, and a ROSES‑2025 proposal focused on subsurface resource detection on the Moon and Mars. Support is requested for limited ETD engineering FTE and HFSS software access to complete these critical modeling tasks.
benefits: Validated 3D dielectric tensor models for Artemis IV-relevant lunar materials to evaluate loss tangent as a function of orientation for potential SAR or GPR radar performance predictions (subsurface resource detection); characterization of complex dielectric permittivity and anisotropy of lunar (NWA 8687) and martian (NWA 11288) samples; research paper for AAS/PSJ; ROSES-2025 proposal; loss tangent data to support U. Tokyo LDA team Artemis IV planning; advancement of waveguide-PNA concept with US Patent Pending status

title: Upright Proprioception Retention via Inflight Training and Evaluation (UPRITE)
lead_organization: Johnson Space Center (JSC) — Houston, Texas
description: This project involves the development of an inflight sensorimotor countermeasure and assessment tool known as the Upright Proprioception Retention via Inflight Training and Evaluation (UPRITE) system. Specifically, an International Space Station (ISS) Technical Demonstration is planned as exploration candidate hardware that can eventually be used for operations. The use of an inflight countermeasure that prevents, or mitigates, the degradation of balance control mechanisms will improve postural stability after transitions to increased gravitational environments. The project described in this document covers a series of steps intended to design and build the hardware to provide such a countermeasure. The UPRITE system targets the sensory subsystems that contribute to the maintenance of balance by requiring subjects to control the tilt angle of the support surface they are standing on. A two-cable subject loading system supplies the force that pulls them toward the tilt-board and real-time feedback of the pitch and roll angles control the position of a cursor on a computer monitor. Two custom training software modules, one presenting successive targets in random locations and the other presenting a single target in continuous motion, challenge the subject to align the cursor with the target. Performance metrics derived from these training exercises will also provide the first onboard assessment targeted toward the sensorimotor system. Validation of the countermeasure’s efficacy is underway during a concurrent bedrest study sponsored by the Human Research Program. The remainder of the activities in this work reflect the steps necessary to create a flight certified version of the hardware and subsequent execution of a Technical Demonstration, using astronaut subjects, on the ISS.
benefits: This effort will enhance current exercise to boost the reliability of sensorimotor capabilities for post-landing activities. Specifically, it aims to provide crewmembers with enhanced sensorimotor re-adaptation with improved proprioceptive function for post-landing critical tasks involving posture and locomotion. These capabilities will enable successful crew performance of exploration mission objectives.

title: Establishing a proto-LTC with Two-Way Satellite Time Transfer (TWSTT) at the Moon
description: This ECI project seeks to address these critical timing needs to develop a system capability for a “proto”- coordinated lunar time (LTC) scale and determine its empirical relationship with the standard terrestrial time scale. Complementary efforts are focused on defining an interoperable framework for communication, PNT, and auxiliary services in cislunar space (known as LunaNet) or advancing low TRL next generation highly stable clock technologies (such as the Spaceflight Compatible Optical Atomic Strontium Ion Clock, or OASIC). This proposed concept is focused on the development of a low small size, weight, and power (low SWaP) clock ensemble using flight-rated COTS parts to be deployed on the lunar surface, and the long-distance twoway satellite time transfer (TWSTT) procedure necessary for defining and tracing the lunar time relationship to UTC. This is a key technological effort because it will establish a feasible means to close the current gap in lunar timing service infrastructure in the next 3-5 years. Systems designed to obtain and distribute measurements of proper lunar time from the lunar surface are needed by lunar PNT systems such as LCRNS. The steady increase in missions going to the Moon will continue to strain the ground station infrastructure to meet cislunar missions’ needs for ranging, Doppler, and timing, when in view. The availability of a timing source providing a stable LTC reference to users on the lunar surface and in orbit can: 1) improve the navigation solutions of cislunar and lunar surface missions, when used as a source for the LunaNet PNT services, thereby unifying the distribution of a common lunar reference system commensurate with LTC; 2) reduce the timing burden on cislunar users by allowing them to use lower SWaP receivers, clocks, and processing power since the LTC time broadcast by the LunaNet Service Provider (LNSP) nodes are orbiting the same central body, are close by, and can more frequently provide time updates through the one-way broadcast; 3) serve as the foundation to establish a common time system for the Moon, analogous to International Atomic Time (TAI) or UTC on Earth.
benefits: The decades ahead will witness monumental advances in the exploration of cislunar space. Following the success of Artemis I and the Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS), subsequent missions will return astronauts, robotic explorers, and science instruments to lunar orbit and the lunar surface, with the goal of establishing an enduring human presence on the Moon and vibrant lunar ecosystem in preparing for Mars. Critical to these endeavors will be establishing a time system at the Moon, to perform experiments of fundamental physics, testing predictions of relativity, and support a permanent presence on the lunar surface and sustained activities from private industry and government. The establishment of a Coordinated Lunar Time (LTC) is essential to enable safe navigation in cislunar space long term and facilitate interoperability between lunar assets and with Earth. The development and maintenance of a LTC at the moon will mature the technology and establish the processes necessary build and maintain a system for Mars. NASA’s Space Communications and Navigation (SCaN) program is working to enhance and develop new network assets for the Artemis program. The Lunar Communications Relay and Navigation System (LCRNS) includes a proposed Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS)-like constellation of relay satellites to provide communication and PNT services primarily at the Moon’s South Pole region. The constellation has three phases of deployment beginning in 2026 and ending in 2029 after the deployment of a minimum of 4 nodes in the constellation. However, the initial LCRNS node(s) may be limited to mathematically defined offsets from the Earth standard Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) which could introduce timing errors, since no proper clock yet exists on the lunar surface to obtain empirical measurements. A clock or ensemble of clocks on the lunar surface can measure a realized time on the lunar geoid and be the first to establish LTC for the Moon. Like the GNSS constellations at Earth, the LCRNS nodes can broadcast the realized LTC time to users on the surface and in cislunar space around the South Pole. In turn, this capability will reduce the Size, Weight, and Power (SWaP) of user’s receiver, clock, and processing requirements for time transfer in the same way GNSS receivers are small and ubiquitous on Earth [5]. The positive outcome to achieve safe navigation based on realized LTC can not be overstated.

title: Hydrogen Peroxide Generation (HPG)
lead_organization: Johnson Space Center (JSC) — Houston, Texas
description: This project focuses on developing and evaluating technologies for in situ hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) generation to support long-duration space missions. Hydrogen peroxide is a versatile disinfectant that can be used for surface cleaning, microbial control, and system sanitization while remaining compatible with Environmental Control and Life Support Systems (ECLSS) and safe for crew exposure. The effort centers on electrochemical production methods that use only water, air, and electricity, eliminating the need to store and transport large quantities of consumables. Two primary approaches are being assessed: a custom-developed cell stack based on prior SBIR work and a commercially available system. Both technologies are evaluated against key performance metrics including concentration, efficiency, durability, mass, power, and volume. A down-selection process will identify the most viable approach for future flight demonstration. Ultimately, this work aims to enable reliable, on-demand disinfectant production to reduce logistics burden and enhance sustainability for exploration-class missions, including lunar and Mars habitats.
benefits: In situ hydrogen peroxide generation provides a significant advantage for space missions by reducing reliance on resupply and enabling on-demand production of a versatile disinfectant using only water, air, and electricity. This capability lowers logistics mass, minimizes stored consumables, and increases operational flexibility by allowing crews to respond immediately to contamination events. Hydrogen peroxide is compatible with life support systems because it decomposes into water and oxygen, avoiding harmful residues in closed-loop environments. It also supports crew health by helping control microbial growth on surfaces and within systems, while offering multiple uses such as surface cleaning, system sanitization, and water stabilization. Overall, this technology enhances mission sustainability, autonomy, and resilience for long-duration exploration missions.

title: Alternate Fecal Container (AFC)
lead_organization: Johnson Space Center (JSC) — Houston, Texas
description: This project provides metabolic waste management technologies for exploration to reduce mass and volume and improve the crew experience. The Alternate Fecal Canister (AFC) is a collapsible alternative to the Hard-Sided Fecal Canister (HFC) provided by the Universal Waste Management System (UWMS) project. The AFC will be tested on the UWMS on ISS when it is restored to operation. The AFC will also fly on Orion's Artemis-3. The AFC is the same size as the HFC so it fits into the UWMS with no modifications to the UWMS. A connection point that hold the item open is added to the HFC lifting mechanism. The AFC weighs about a pound less than the HFC and can be collapsed for empty stowage saving space for up-mass.
benefits: Reductions in mass and volume for metabolic waste management increase available space for other cargo, both for science and crew comfort. For long duration exploration missions, the number of collection devices and consumables like wipes and gloves adds up based on the number of crewmembers and the number of days and quickly becomes a large number. Making the canisters used for collection and storage of the fecal waste lighter helps in spacecraft design.

title: Off Planet Laundromat
lead_organization: Ames Research Center (ARC) — Moffett Field, California
description: The State of the Art (SOA) is to de-orbit commercial garments and to return spacesuit materials to Earth. The up-mass involved is unsustainable for long duration missions such as to Mars and thus reduces mission capability. Soiled materials are not appreciated by astronauts, and they create health hazards to skin and other organ systems from bio-loads and bio-aerosols. Here we leverage two new commercial approaches: one using low water methods coupled with ozone disinfection and enhanced detergents for commercial garments, and liquid CO 2 dry cleaning for space materials and electronics that are degraded by water. The latter would be used on the Martian surface where MOXIE has already concentrated atmospheric CO 2 , and potentially the lunar surface where CO 2 is found in lunar CO 2 cold trips. Objectives To develop low mass, effective flight hardware and protocols for cleaning both commercial garments worn by astronauts as well as specialized space suit materials. End-State Lab-proven hardware for both methods on current and future materials ready for test flights.
benefits: The primary benefit is logistics reduction, secondarily astronaut health and well being.

title: Formaldehyde Monitor
lead_organization: Johnson Space Center (JSC) — Houston, Texas
description: Formaldehyde (HCHO) is a mucosal irritant generated by off-gassing and metabolic processes and is closely tracked during human spaceflight, as the acceptable limit for crew exposure is low. HCHO monitoring is a requirement for all Moon-to-Mars programs, particularly as the potential for dormancy and lowered pressures in Exploration vehicles could lead to increased off-gassing of HCHO. However, the legacy NASA methods for HCHO detection in spacecraft, which depend on sample return for analysis and only provide concentrations averaged over multiple days, are unsuitable for future missions, where a real-time insight into the HCHO concentration is necessary to ensure the safety of crew members. Efforts have been undertaken previously to develop this type of monitor, but issues with 1) lack of sensitivity, 2) calibration lifetime, and/or 3) interferences from other atmospheric gases have consistently remained as shortfalls. The Formaldehyde Monitor development will consolidate an understanding of state-of-the-art formaldehyde monitoring instrumentation utilizing different technologies, evaluate those technologies while also continuing to support the development of a handheld instrument based on technology with spaceflight heritage.
benefits: The development of a small, handheld formaldehyde monitor will be useful for meeting the trace contaminant requirements of all upcoming Artemis missions as well as Moon Base. Specifically, this monitor will provide a heretofore unavailable ability to monitor for formaldehyde during first ingress of vehicles/modules. Formaldehyde is a known off-gassing compound with low exposure limits that can serve as a “canary” for other potential off-gassing products, making this instrument particularly important. Additionally, the technology would allow for the detection of other toxic small molecules, such as hydrazine.

title: Iodine Removal Hot Side
lead_organization: Johnson Space Center (JSC) — Houston, Texas
description: Mars Campaign Office (MCO) Life Support Systems project Wastewater Processing and Water Management projects develop technologies to collect, store and process wastewater as well as manage the water recovered. Within an integrated life support system, water recovery systems provide water for use by various environmental control and life support functions on board the spacecraft. These functions may include drinking water, food re-hydration, water for crew hygiene, flush water for the spacecraft urinal, source water for oxygen generation, and, depending on the complexity of the life support system, water for crew shower and laundry. The wastewater streams that return from these uses and require treatment to be returned back to a potable state can include stabilized urine and flush water, humidity condensate, shower and laundry grey water, and water from carbon dioxide and wet-trash processing systems. The purpose of the water recovery system is to close the water loop by removing the contaminants associated with the various wastewater streams and then returning the balance of clean water back to the potable water bus in a stabilized form suitable for storage and reuse. Iodine Removal Hot Side project is the development of technology to remove iodine from the hot side of the Potable Water System. This project is focused on the development of advanced water filtration media that has broad application for the efficient removal of water contaminants in spacecraft water systems. It also considers re-engineering water system to reduce the water volumes that may not include a biocide. Overall, this technology development will ensure the biocide disinfects a majority of the hot water portion of the potable water system while removing iodine prior to crew consumption.
benefits: This technology ensures iodine efficacy within the hot water portion of the dispenser as well as safe removal of the iodine prior to consumption.

title: Biofilms
lead_organization: Johnson Space Center (JSC) — Houston, Texas
description: Mars Campaign Office (MCO) Life Support Systems Wastewater Processing and Water Management projects develop technologies to collect, store and process wastewater as well as manage the water recovered. Within an integrated life support system, water recovery systems provide water for use by various environmental control and life support functions on board the spacecraft. These functions may include drinking water, food re-hydration, water for crew hygiene, flush water for the spacecraft urinal, source water for oxygen generation, and, depending on the complexity of the life support system, water for crew shower and laundry. The wastewater streams that return from these uses and require treatment to be returned back to a potable state can include stabilized urine and flush water, humidity condensate, shower and laundry grey water, and water from carbon dioxide and wet-trash processing systems. The purpose of the water recovery system is to close the water loop by removing the contaminants associated with the various wastewater streams and then returning the balance of clean water back to the potable water bus in a stabilized form suitable for storage and reuse. This project is investigating biofilm mitigations in the waste water to prevent growth of biofilms generated by microbes and fungi which can foul the water processing system. Biofilm mitigations include the following Nutrient filtration resin to reduce growth of biofilms in the wastewater tank. Ultraviolet (UV) Disinfection UV transmitted via fiber optics to reduce growth of biofilms in the wastewater tank. Aeration Module introduces a managed microbial population to treat the organic loading in the condensate which is sent to the wastewater tank.
benefits: Prevents interruption of water processing by mitigating biofilm growth in the wastewater tank.

title: Silver Biocide
lead_organization: Johnson Space Center (JSC) — Houston, Texas
description: Mars Campaign Office (MCO) Life Support Systems Wastewater Processing and Water Management project develops technologies to collect, store and process wastewater as well as manage the water recovered. Within an integrated life support system, water recovery systems provide water for use by various environmental control and life support functions on board the spacecraft. These functions may include drinking water, food re-hydration, water for crew hygiene, flush water for the spacecraft urinal, source water for oxygen generation, and, depending on the complexity of the life support system, water for crew shower and laundry. The wastewater streams that return from these uses and require treatment to be returned back to a potable state can include stabilized urine and flush water, humidity condensate, shower and laundry grey water, and water from carbon dioxide and wet-trash processing systems. The purpose of the water recovery system is to close the water loop by removing the contaminants associated with the various wastewater streams and then returning the balance of clean water back to the potable water bus in a stabilized form suitable for storage and reuse. This project is investigating the use of silver biocide to control water quality. Silver Foam Doser is a passive silver ion releasing foam. It was developed as a way of metering the safe range of silver the crew can consume and still inhibit microbial growth in drinking water.
benefits: A biocide that does not have to be removed and can be safely consumed by the crew.

title: Nitrogen Resupply
lead_organization: Johnson Space Center (JSC) — Houston, Texas
description: Mars Campaign Office Life Support Systems is working on technologies for future Lunar and Martian missions. Nitrogen gas is a major constituent used for a mixed gas environment to mitigate flammability in the cabin. Cabin pressure control maintenance from hatch losses and re-pressurization from Extra Vehicular Activities (EVA) are key activities on a spacecraft that require make up nitrogen. Currently, the State of the Art method to resupply nitrogen is by tanks which poses a significant mass and volume constraint to a mission. The Nitrogen Resupply project has explored two alternative methods: 1. Decomposition of Nitrous Oxide to recuperate the Nitrogen. 2. Recovery of gaseous Nitrogen from Cryogenic Nitrogen tanks.
benefits: Reduces the launch mass and volume constraints of taking makeup Nitrogen in tanks.

title: Medical Oxygen (MedOx)
lead_organization: Johnson Space Center (JSC) — Houston, Texas
description: The Medical Oxygen (MedOx) Project is in support of the Mars Campaign Office, part of the Life Support Systems portfolio. MedOx is supporting the needs for bridging the gap for medical exploration needs when it comes to oxygen needs for the crew during respiratory distress. The current state of the art is by means of oxygen tanks supplied for missions to the International Space Station (ISS). These tanks, although reliable for providing high purity oxygen, take up by mass and volume within storage of these tanks, along with adding additional pressure within the cabin if ever released. The MedOx project is solely focused on portable oxygen concentrators to provide both the flow rate and percentage of oxygen needed for a wide variety of respiratory prescriptions. Oxygen concentrators provide the means to maintain continuous flow rates, high purity of oxygen, and become a net zero process, which does not introduce new pressure variables into the habitable volume. Both laboratory testing and environmental testing that meet program level requirements are underway with devices that are prime candidates.
benefits: Less Mass and Volume Constraints High purity Oxygen Production Portable

title: Flight-Like Advanced Materials Reactor (FLAMR)
lead_organization: Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) — Huntsville, Alabama
description: The National Research Council's "NASA Space Technology Roadmaps and Priorities" identified long-duration environmental control and life support systems (ECLSS) as one of the top five areas capable of having the greatest impact on deep space exploration. The capability addressed represents an advanced system to further close the atmosphere revitalization loop on long duration human spacecraft. NASA Space Technology Roadmap TA 6 “Human Health, Life Support and Habitation Systems” established for the technology performance goal of increasing the percentage of oxygen recovered from metabolic carbon dioxide to 75-90%. As future exploration missions extend beyond Low Earth Orbit (LEO), vehicles will require life support systems (LSS) with high reliability and self-sufficiency, as practical opportunities for consumable resupply will not exist. An effective life support system must maintain a safe and habitable atmosphere within a spacecraft by removing contaminants while simultaneously maintaining the proper atmospheric composition and cabin pressure. The goal of this effort is to advance the state-of-the-art of atmospheric revitalization system technologies required to enable NASA’s human exploration missions. Honeywell International, Inc. developed the Methane Pyrolysis Brassboard between 2017 and 2021 which has an O 2 recovery rate of up to 95%. The Brassboard included metallic reactors. Due to the high operating temperatures, it was determined that the reactors should be made of advanced materials to extend the operating lifecycle of the system. Honeywell International Inc. then began further work to provide two Flight-Like Advanced Material reactors (FLAMR) to advance the methane pyrolysis technology. The period of performance of this contract is August 02, 2021 through August 2, 2026. This most recent contract aims to design a low-mass, low-heat-loss flight-like reactor that can withstand the high temperatures required by the Methane Pyrolysis process, with a focus on materials of construction and thermal management. A 6-month extension of this contract is planned for the end of FY26 through the beginning of FY27. The extension will cover preliminary work towards development of a Flight Prototype. There are plans to contract with Honeywell Aerospace, Inc., a recent spin off of Honeywell International, Inc., to develop a Flight Prototype of the system beginning FY27. The system will include the FLAMR reactors along with the ancillary hardware that make up the system.
benefits: Along with the Sabatier, the CVD/MPS system has a theoretical oxygen (O 2 ) recovery of 95% from metabolic carbon dioxide (CO 2 ).This level of O2 recovery could eliminate the need for re-supply of Oxygen/water making long duration flight possible.

title: Exploration Aerosol Monitors (ExAM)
lead_organization: Johnson Space Center (JSC) — Houston, Texas
description: The Mars Campaign Office (MCO) Life Support Systems project Environmental Monitoring (EM) systems task objectives are to develop and demonstrate onboard monitoring, detection, and analysis capabilities that will replace the state-of-the-art (SOA) need to frequently return air samples to Earth for ground-based laboratory analysis. This effort is addressing these challenges by adopting new analytical technologies and techniques that will allow for a modular EM system architecture that integrates multiple sensing modalities to address the monitoring needs of future deep-space exploration missions. Exploration Aerosol Monitors (ExAM): Provides a flight demonstration of multiple aerosol monitors to measure and characterize particles in the crew respiratory hazard range. The suite of aerosol sensors will collect passive samples, as well as detect, measure, and distinguish aerosols of varied sizes and types.
benefits: The Aerosol Monitors suite of instruments are candidates for exploration missions and the ISS deployments will raise the technology readiness levels (TRL) and provide insight and lessons learned for the next generation of spacecraft dust monitors. OPERA has the unique ability to distinguish between different types of particles, which can assist smoke detection and prevent false alarms from dust in a coordinated monitoring architecture. The MARS samplers provide gravimetric verification for any dust monitoring activity, with archival samples that can be analyzed with a variety of techniques offline. Respirable lunar dust particles are a threat to human health and dust monitoring technologies provide the following benefits: (1) track exposure levels for human health protection and requirements verification, (2) Validate dust mitigation technologies used in lunar missions, (3) Alert to failures in HEPA filtration or other ECLSS equipment.

title: Spacecraft Water Impurities Monitor (SWIM)
lead_organization: Johnson Space Center (JSC) — Houston, Texas
description: The Mars Campaign Office (MCO) Life Support Systems project Environmental Monitoring (EM) systems task objectives are to develop and demonstrate onboard monitoring, detection, and analysis capabilities that will replace the state-of-the-art (SOA) need to frequently return water samples to Earth for ground-based laboratory analysis. This effort is addressing these challenges by adopting new analytical technologies and techniques that will allow for a modular EM system architecture that integrates multiple sensing modalities to address the monitoring needs of future deep-space exploration missions. Spacecraft Water Impurities Monitor (SWIM): The development of an in-flight water quality monitor for organic and inorganic impurities to protect crew health and vehicle hardware.
benefits: •Provides in-flight identification and quantification of a wide range of organic and inorganic species of concern to the toxicology, Environmental Control and Life Support Systems (ECLSS), and Extra-Vehicular Activity (EVA) communities. •Allows for near real-time sample analysis, providing on-demand data to mission managers. Knowledge of contaminant amounts and identities has a twofold impact: •Enables cognizant, risk-based decision making with respect to go/no-go for water use (e.g. crew consumption, space suit loading). •Allows for sensible diagnosis of off-nominal ECLSS performance.

title: Mini Total Organic Carbon Analyzer (MiniTOCA)
lead_organization: Johnson Space Center (JSC) — Houston, Texas
description: The Mars Campaign Office (MCO) Life Support Systems project Environmental Monitoring (EM) systems task objectives are to develop and demonstrate onboard monitoring, detection, and analysis capabilities that will replace the state-of-the-art (SOA) need to frequently returning water samples to Earth for ground-based laboratory analysis. This effort is addressing these challenges by adopting new analytical technologies and techniques that will allow for a modular EM system architecture that integrates sensing modalities to address the monitoring needs of future deep-space exploration missions. Mini Total Organic Carbon Analyzer (MiniTOCA) - Develop a smaller version of Total Organic Carbon Analyzer (TOCA). Reduce the mass, volume and consumable shelf life and maintain functionality to determine water portability for both crew drinking water and (Extra Vehicular Activity) EVA. A novel UV technology and tunable laser spectrometer was developed for CO2 detection.
benefits: Novel Core technologies allow for the reduction of consumable mass as well as overall system mass power and volume.

title: Four Bed CO2 Scrubber
lead_organization: Johnson Space Center (JSC) — Houston, Texas
description: The Four Bed Carbon Dioxide (ops nom FBCO2) Scrubber has been developed as a technology demonstration flight system for the purpose of evaluating its potential as a carbon dioxide removal technology for the International Space Station (ISS) and future missions to the Moon and Mars. It was launched in August 2021 and activated in September of 2021. The operation of a FBCO2 can be explained with the aid of the schematic shown in Figure 1. The FBCO2 continuously removes carbon dioxide (CO2) from the atmosphere. The four beds consist of two desiccant beds and two CO2 sorbent beds. The system operates such that one desiccant bed and one CO2 sorbent bed are adsorbing while the other two beds are desorbing. When a new half cycle begins, the beds switch sorbent modes. The incoming air stream to the FBCO2 is downstream of a condensing heat exchanger and has a dewpoint and dry bulb temperature between 40 and 60 degF. The air stream passes first through a desiccant bed to remove much of the moisture from the process air. The temperature of the air stream rises as it flows through the desiccant bed due to the heat of adsorption. The process air is next drawn through the system blower and then through an air-liquid (coolant water) heat exchanger or precooler. The precooler increases CO2 sorbent efficiency by reducing process air temperature before entering the CO2 sorbent bed. Prior to returning to the cabin, the air stream passes through the desiccant bed that adsorbed moisture from the previous half cycle. The water loaded desiccant bed desorbs this moisture to the air stream and returns it to the cabin atmosphere. This is called a water-save system, in contrast to the 2-bed Skylab system, which vented adsorbed water to space.
benefits: • Provides increased CO₂‑removal performance over the state‑of‑the‑art, the ISS Tech Demo has demonstrated increase performance over the SOA. • Delivers higher reliability for long‑duration and exploration missions, meeting the need for CO₂‑removal systems with increased reliability and performance and reduced mass. • Supports closed‑loop atmospheric revitalization architectures as the Four Bed CO₂ Scrubber Closed Loop Build, enabling reduced logistics and increased oxygen recovery. • Closes critical exploration reliability gaps, FBCO₂ demonstrates potential solutions for highly reliable systems that can meet performance requirements for Exploration. • Enables integrated system testing and ground capability retention, with Environmental Control and Life Support Systems (ECLSS) Evolution confirming that ground testbeds increase reliability dataset, reducing risk for Exploration missions. • Provides a pathway for infusion into future platforms, including use as baseline system for Mars Transit Habitat, potential backup to Gateway systems, and interest from Commercial LEO Destinations (CLD) partners for design packages. • Supports reduced mass, volume, and long‑term power consumption, with ongoing Calnetix blower and controller upgrades and associated development planning. • Extends operational life and reduces logistic risk by transitioning to sustained ISS operations and continuing through ISS end‑of‑life, providing long‑term data for reliability and maintainability.

title: eXploration Potable Water Dispenser Build (xPWD)
lead_organization: Johnson Space Center (JSC) — Houston, Texas
description: The xPWD is a next‑generation Exploration Potable Water Dispenser designed to improve water dispensing capability on the International Space Station (ISS) and serve as a technology pathfinder for Artemis transit and surface habitats. The system is a technology demonstration funded by the ISS Exploration Environmental Control and Life Support (ECLS) Integration Office, targeting improvements over the legacy PWD including: Elimination of stagnant “dead‑leg” water loops that drove microbial risk in the original PWD Implementation of UV‑LED disinfection to reduce consumables and enable sterilization after dormancy Support for increasing ISS crew complements and higher rehydration demand
benefits: Core technical objectives are: Demonstrate reliable potable‑water dispensing in microgravity using a simplified hydraulic architecture Evaluate UV‑LED–based microbial control as a flight‑viable replacement for iodine biocide systems Characterize performance after extended dormancy periods , including reactivation procedures and water quality evolution Validate automated dispensing hardware and controls , including Data Acquisition (DAQ), solenoid valves, pressure sensing, and button‑press actuators Support Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog (CHAPEA) habitat operations , including Total Organic Carbon (TOC)/Total Inorganic Carbon (TIC) water‑quality trending and microbiology verification

title: Mars Exercise System
lead_organization: Johnson Space Center (JSC) — Houston, Texas
description: Current exercise countermeasure systems (CMS) for long-duration spaceflight are not sufficient to meet both the complex health needs of crews on extended stays while also adhering to the strict requirements for mass, volume, and power for future long-duration exploration missions to the moon or Mars. This project will identify Exercise Capabilities requirements associated with musculoskeletal, aerobic, and sensorimotor health maintenance for long duration space travel as well as durations on the Martian surface, as well as the Gaps in requirement rationale. A Gap Closure Plan will be developed and followed during this multi-year project to converge on strictly necessary requirements backed by evidence from research data. Technology gaps will be identified between state-of-the-art technology and needs, and these gaps will be addressed through thoughtful development of subsystem technology. Human-in-the-loop testing will be used to evaluate feasibility and efficacy of subsystems, and requirements will be updated accordingly. Physiologic monitoring tools will also be integrated and/or developed, and software decision support tools will be investigated and potentially advanced as well. Adjunct countermeasure technology will be researched, integrated, developed, and evaluated, including any that may multiply the effectiveness of other countermeasure technology given certain mass, power, volume, and other requirements. Rehabilitation subsystem capabilities will also be investigated for potential subsystem development. Resulting evaluation data from subsystem testing and analysis may lead to development and integration of a multimodal system, which may in turn serve as a NASA reference system for the production of Mars program vehicle requirements and eventual spaceflight countermeasure system, or even as a potential option for future downselect consideration. The project will ultimately seek to develop a Mars-focused exercise countermeasure system to meet programmatic requirements for protecting crew health and physical performance abilities within a Mars Transit and Surface Exploration mission design. Comprised of Engineering and Exercise Science experts at Johnson Space Center, the project team will draw on historical knowledge, the existing database of spaceflight health and performance outcomes relative to in-flight countermeasure implementation, current subject matter expert (SME) experience in developing and implementing exercise countermeasures, as well as prospective mission architecture documentation to baseline a set of design requirements for the exercise system and its capabilities. These capabilities will include resistance, aerobic, and sensorimotor exercise training of various modalities to allow for the execution of a comprehensive set of prescriptions, as well as integrated software, a graphical user interface, and the ability to integrate with performance monitoring systems (i.e., aerobic capacity monitor). The Exercise Physiology and Countermeasures (EPC) laboratory will develop and baseline functional requirements for a Mars Transit vehicle CMS aiming to maintain multi-system health and performance of all crewmembers across outbound and return mission phases. Additionally, the JSC Engineering team will assess the latest available Mars design reference mission information and vehicle architecture, as well as other representative vehicle constraints, to generate best estimates for assumptions/constraints that will define design parameters, such as those related to mass, power, volume, thermal, acoustic, vibration, and electromagnetic compatibility.
benefits: This effort will baseline and revise the Exercise Capabilities requirements for a Mars design reference mission; identify and address requirements gaps with an evidence-based approach; identify technology gaps associated with the baselined requirements (including those related to aerobic monitoring); integrate and develop subsystem technologies to address these gaps; and evaluate these advancements in technology through human-in-the-loop studies. Resulting evaluation data from subsystem testing and analysis may lead to development and integration of a multimodal system, which may in turn serve as a NASA reference system for the production of Mars program vehicle requirements and eventual spaceflight countermeasure system, or even as a potential option for future downselect consideration. Ultimately, this project will develop the technology necessary, and currently lacking, to provide a candidate countermeasure system for crew health maintenance during a Mars design reference mission.

title: Mars Portable Life Support System Testbed (PLSS Testbed)
lead_organization: Johnson Space Center (JSC) — Houston, Texas
description: To get from Moon to Mars, development of a Mars-centered spacesuit to support extravehicular activity (EVA) must begin now. In an effort towards this goal, setup of a Mars Portable Life Support System (PLSS) team to evaluate schematics for a Mars Extravehicular Mobility Unit (MxEMU) is underway. As part of a previous study, a wide range of potential architectures were evaluated and compared to determine leading options for a Martian PLSS. Going forward, these schematics will inform technology development, testing, detailed sizing analysis, and feasibility studies. A Mars PLSS Test Bed will be developed and used to assess the schematics on a breadboard style configuration of components.
benefits: The Mars PLSS Testbed will build an integrated system to evaluate schematics for a Mars PLSS, leading to a Mars spacesuit development.

title: Mars 2020 Ground Test Unit (GTU)
lead_organization: Johnson Space Center (JSC) — Houston, Texas
description: On the Mars Perseverance rover, a suite of five spacesuit materials is being exposed to the environment and spectroscopy data is being taken by the SHERLOC (Scanning Habitable Environments with Raman & Luminescence for Organics & Chemicals) instrument. This project will: (1) Secure a corresponding ground test experiment repeating this exposure in a simulated Mars chamber; (2) Evaluate exposed materials for changes; and (3) Correlate in-situ vs. experimental spectroscopy SHERLOC data.
benefits: This project will provide improved understanding of the effect that Mars radiation has on currently used and candidate materials, not only for space suits but other surface assets including rovers and habitats.

title: Advanced Trace Contaminant Control
lead_organization: Johnson Space Center (JSC) — Houston, Texas
description: Trace Contaminant Control (TCC) is typically activated carbon and some level of catalyst to adsorb and react contaminants in the air phase. The current state-of-the-art carbon dioxide (CO2) removal sorbents utilize amines that rely on a hard vacuum to desorb during an Extravehicular Activity (EVA). Some sorbents also act to remove some trace contaminants. This may be severely limited on Mars due to the atmosphere. Therefore, Mars will require new methods, sorbents, and testing of the current and new and novel technologies to assess feasibility on Mars. New technologies for regenerable TCC have been developed, but have not been tested in a direct manner. This project will complete a technology comparison of new TCC technologies for use in next generation spacesuit portable life support systems (PLSS). The current TCC is a large consumable item, and multiple spares will have to be sent with downtime for replacements. The primary driver for a new technology is mass and lifespan. Volume is a secondary driver, as is pressure drop. Multiple companies have produced TCC sorbents and CO2 removal technologies for the Space Suit. This project intends to evaluate these advanced technologies at a Mars atmosphere for infusion and down selection in the PLSS.
benefits: This project will verify that vacuum regenerable trace contaminant control sorbents and CO2 removal technologies will work in a simulated environment. Implementation of regenerable TCCs as part of the PLSS will reduce consumables and deliver a smaller lighter weight PLSS far more suitable for the Martian surface than current designs.

title: Food Packaging Validation
lead_organization: Johnson Space Center (JSC) — Houston, Texas
description: The food system currently requires two layers of packaging on freeze-dried and low moisture foods to provide adequate barrier to oxygen and moisture and maintain vacuum integrity through the required 3-5 year shelf life. A new package has been identified with the potential to replace the two-layer package currently used for freeze-dried and low moisture foods, which if successful could reduce packaging mass and eliminate cumbersome layers of trash from these foods. This project will validate representative food sets stored in the new packaging system for quality and acceptability, as well as packaging depress-repress survivability.
benefits: This project has the potential to reduce packaging up-mass and eliminate cumbersome layers of trash for all vehicle foods systems.

title: BioMole Preparation (PowerBlade)
lead_organization: Johnson Space Center (JSC) — Houston, Texas
description: As NASA progresses to longer, farther, and more complex destinations, providing our crew members with a safe and healthy environment is essential to mission success. Our current process for microbial surface sampling includes returning samples to be processed and analyzed on the ground. Martian missions will not include sample return, so we must ensure the crew can handle and analyze samples within their habitat. The Exploration Medical Integrated Product Team (XMIPT), in conjunction with the NASA Microbiology Lab at Johnson Space Center, have created an innovative solution to address this issue. The development of BioMole Prep addresses these concerns by automating sample preparation. This change reduces the chances of human error, and the length of time crew must spend processing samples from five hours to two, allows for more complex analysis, and can allow crew to respond quickly while making health care and environmental related decisions.
benefits: Samples critical to maintaining a healthy environment will be analyzed in real time, enabling the crew to respond promptly to any environmental concerns or changes. This technology enables additional data to be collected, allowing for more informed and autonomous risk assessments to be performed by crewmembers and ground teams.

title: In Situ Lab Analysis
lead_organization: Glenn Research Center (GRC) — Cleveland, Ohio
description: Exploration missions will feature austere habitable environments, volume and mass constraints, limited to no resupply, and communication delays that will impose challenges to evaluating and maintaining crew health and performance. Due to increased exposure to the hazards of human space flight and the lack of evacuation capabilities, exploration missions will demand increasingly detailed coordination of medical care between crewmembers and care providers despite the decreasing availability of real-time communications. This asynchronous, Earth-independent mode of operation also necessitates one or more in-flight crew and ground support will have to assess, diagnose, and treat medical conditions that may arise in an efficient and effective manner. Exploration missions will have constraints in mass, volume, power, consumables and resupply missions, leaving crew with the inability to return biological samples back to Earth for analysis. In the current low earth orbit (LEO) paradigm, most samples are obtained pre/post flight or down-massed for analysis. This will not be feasible for extended duration missions to the moon and Mars. This, combined with the need to operate with greater autonomy compared to a lunar or LEO mission, necessitate point-of-care medical diagnostic technology, specifically, a suite of in-situ lab analysis devices will be needed to manage medical conditions in real-time. The objective of this project is to identify the lowest mass/volume solutions for an exploration lab suite capable of measuring high yield clinical analytes. Evaluations will include ground and in-flight testing of selected devices. In-flight testing of selected devices will evaluate their ability to operate in the microgravity environment, their measurement accuracy, and their usability.
benefits: Providing an in-situ lab analysis capability will enable both operational and research needs to minimize risk to overall crew health and performance and help to characterize and better understand how the effects of extended deep space environments affect the health and performance of crew. In-situ clinical lab analysis would enable screening, diagnosis, and monitoring of medical conditions without frequent resupply or sample return. Development and testing of point-of-care lab analysis is also an interest area for the DoD and has applications for advancing global and remote healthcare. Point-of-care lab analysis is also of interest in terrestrial areas that are remote with limited access to healthcare resources (i.e. polar medicine, developing nations).

title: Portable ECG Device
lead_organization: Johnson Space Center (JSC) — Houston, Texas
description: As NASA prepares for longer duration missions that will take us farther than ever before, we must prioritize our most valuable spaceflight asset: humans. Future Martian missions present a new set of challenges, including communication delays that could be harmful if a crew member faced a medical situation and needed care. While we must consider humans first, other factors such as vehicle space, consumables, and ease of use play a role in the medical hardware we send with our crews. This project seeks to make the health and safety of crew members easier to monitor and respond to, should the need arise for emergency care.
benefits: Due to its small size and ease of use, selected portable ECG hardware addresses many of the challenges medical devices often present during spaceflight missions. Medical capabilities for the crew require a large amount of space for hardware, consumables, and durable medical equipment, and often require medical professionals to interpret results. The Kardia 12 lead (12L) ECG system selected for analysis can quickly share raw data via email or cloud, negating the need for multiple teams of people to respond to a medical event. Crew members can receive data directly from the device, store it, transmit it to flight surgeons on the ground, and better understand the health status of crew members. This system is compact, low mass, and requires fewer consumables than traditional ECG monitoring systems, which are desirable characteristics as we seek to optimize medical capabilities for long duration missions.

title: Clinical Decision Support
lead_organization: Johnson Space Center (JSC) — Houston, Texas
description: The Clinical Decision Support (CDS) Project is a NASA initiative to enable safe, autonomous medical care for crews on future Lunar Base, Mars transit, and Mars surface missions, where communication delays and blackouts will preclude real-time guidance from Earth. Under these conditions, astronauts must independently detect, diagnose, and treat medical events, even when no physician is onboard and crew medical training time is limited. This project integrates clinical, human factors, and software engineering expertise into a unified CDS strategy. Core objectives include surveying commercial and government CDS tools, defining requirements for spaceflight-relevant functions, and formulating a technology development plan for tailored or internally developed solutions that can operate reliably with constrained computing resources and intermittent connectivity. The CDS capability will be validated through progressive ground testing and eventual flight demonstration, with tight integration with the Crew Exploration Health Portal (CEHP) and the Crew Health and Performance Integrated Data System Platform (CHP‑IDSP) to capture clinical data, support asynchronous consultation with flight surgeons, and sustain earth‑independent medical operations.
benefits: Today’s current low earth orbit paradigm of the International Space Station (ISS)’s medical care depends on real-time communication with ground flight surgeons and a large support team. This model will not be viable for Mars missions with up to 45‑minute round‑trip communication delays, communication blackouts, and limited to no evacuation and resupplies. A spaceflight CDS tool will help crew members with varying levels of medical training initiate timely, evidence-informed diagnosis and treatment during the critical first 1–2 hours of care, rather than waiting for delayed ground input. By guiding patient histories, vital signs collection, focused physical examinations, selection of feasible diagnostics, and safe initial therapies, the CDS is expected to improve medical outcomes, reduce preventable errors, and lower overall risk to crew health and performance. Preliminary analyses indicate such a system can effectively augment crew cognitive capability and scope of practice, decreasing projected mission medical risk for long-duration deep space expeditions.

title: Surface Power Exchange Vehicle Interface
lead_organization: Johnson Space Center (JSC) — Houston, Texas
description: The Surface Element Power Exchange Vehicle Interface project is establishing a unified, bidirectional 6kW (120 V, 50 A) power interface for all lunar and future Martian surface elements. This standard interface will enable any surface assets—such as habitats, rovers, power plants, or technology payloads—to exchange power with other elements, sources, or loads through a common interface. The project scope includes defining functions, requirements, and attributes, that mature the development of a standardized power interface that supports safe and reliable bidirectional power flow while meeting existing space power standards and lunar power specifications. This effort includes drafting an interface requirements document, incorporating industry feedback, producing an interface control document, and supporting verification of the finalized power interface. By standardizing this power exchange interface across all surface systems, the project will ensure interoperability, reduce integration complexity, and streamline logistics for sustained lunar—and eventually Martian—surface operations.
benefits: This project will deliver a standardized power exchange interface for all Artemis surface elements, enabling any element to safely send or receive power from another. By providing comprehensive design specifications through an Interface Requirements Document and Interface Control Document, the project allows Moon‑to‑Mars programs, international partners, and commercial vendors to design hardware to a common set of specifications, improving interoperability, reducing integration risk, and simplifying end‑to‑end system planning. Key technical considerations and performance parameters include: Electrical Isolation: The interface will support configurable isolation between EPS and EPCE supply and return conductors to prevent circulating AC or DC currents and mitigate stability concerns when multiple sources and loads operate in parallel. Isolation levels will meet or exceed 1 MΩ at the hardware level, ensuring that a fault in one branch of the EPS or EPCE does not disable the other source. Distribution Wiring: The interface will implement a two‑wire power distribution system with a dedicated return conductor, maintaining a distributed single‑point ground and preventing intentional current flow through spacecraft structure. Parallel wiring for current sharing remains compatible, and minimizing conductor spacing is recommended to reduce inductance. Single‑Point Ground: Grounding architecture will be coordinated closely with Moon‑to‑Mars programs to ensure compliance and compatibility across all participating systems. Autonomous functions using Robotics technology: The connector system will support the use of robotics technology to help the manipulation and mate / de-mate of the surface power connector system between two vehicles.

title: Advanced Energy Management System
lead_organization: Glenn Research Center (GRC) — Cleveland, Ohio
description: The Advanced Energy Management System (AEMS) project is developing an autonomous energy management capability for future lunar and Martian surface power networks. As surface operations expand beyond isolated, self-sufficient systems, AEMS continues to provide the controls, communications, and interoperability needed to manage complex power generation, storage, distribution, and system constraints with minimal to no human intervention. AEMS will: Coordinate power sharing among surface elements, including bidirectional transfer for Moon‑to‑Mars architectures. Manage survival-power distribution during extended darkness using dedicated backup sources. Integrate and control multiple power sources and loads across large-scale commercial and exploration power grids. Automatically incorporates new power sources, switchgears, and loads without operator input. Predict future power needs and take corrective actions—such as prioritized load shedding—to ensure critical systems remain powered. Optimize energy storage operations to reduce losses and enhance system resilience, security, and reliability. The project implements real-time control of heterogeneous power assets, including Vertical Solar Array Technology (VSAT) units, Fission Surface Power (FSP) systems, and energy storage devices such as batteries and fuel cells. AEMS ensures robust, continuous operation and effective contingency management, particularly during lunar night and other extended darkness periods, while maintaining system health and operational constraints.
benefits: AEMS reduces the impact of insufficient power or energy—especially during faults or failures—and limits disruptions to critical and high‑priority loads, such as blackouts and brownouts. These benefits are measured through three key performance metrics: Hours of Load Shed, Hours of Unserved Energy, and System Reliability. Hours of Load Shed The total time the power system must deviate from the approved schedule and reduce power to loads that were planned to receive it. Load shedding may occur due to: an incorrect power budget provided to the scheduler. an inaccurate load‑flow analysis that overestimates allowable power and underestimates distribution losses. A failure that causes a reduction in available power. Hours of Unserved Energy The total time when sufficient energy was available but not scheduled. This metric captures cases where the control algorithm under‑allocates power, helping ensure power budgets accurately account for usage and distribution losses. System Reliability The availability of power to critical loads (roughly the top 20% of loads). Following a fault or failure, the system must automatically reconfigure to maintain power to these loads. A reliability of 99.99% (“four nines”) corresponds to less than 53 minutes of lost power per year. The Mars performance target of 99.999% (“five nines”) corresponds to less than 5 minutes per year. For deep‑space vehicles—such as a Mars transit spacecraft with up to a 45‑minute communication latency—any single failure affecting a critical load could significantly reduce system reliability due to operator notification, diagnosis, and recovery time.

title: Crew Clothing Textiles
lead_organization: Johnson Space Center (JSC) — Houston, Texas
description: The Specialized Crew Clothing Textile Development for Exploration project focuses on the development, testing, and production of non-flammable knit textiles for Intravehicular Activity (IVA) crew clothing in the Exploration Atmosphere (up to 37% O2/8.2 psia), intended for infusion and use in Artemis missions and beyond. Some of the textiles with Crew Clothing applications include sewing threads, comfortable woven fabrics, and next-to-skin and exercise clothing knit fabrics. The textiles developed through this project could vary based on the agency’s most urgent fire-resistant (FR) textile needs. The NASA Engineering and Safety Center (NESC) led an agency-wide technical assessment of NASA's FR textile gaps. They released a report with their findings and identified Tier 1 (high-priority) and Tier 2 (lower-priority) textiles based on current agency needs and priorities. The report includes a recommended strategy for closing the FR textile gaps. Each textile development effort will have the same general approach starting with a Commercial-off-the-Shelf (COTS) evaluation (Phase 0) to benchmark the State-of-the-Art (SOA) in a specific textile category. Modified-COTS solutions will be investigated for feasibility to determine if a full development effort is needed. Then there will be planning and baselining (Phase 1) to define requirements, schedule, contract needs, and a testing plan. A contract mechanism will be put in place with a selected vendor for modified-COTS or prototype development (Phase 2). When the prototyping is completed and all requirements are met, a final production run (Phase 3) will be done to establish part numbers and production parameters with the vendor so the textile can be reliably procured in the future for infusion into exploration class missions. Fiscal Year 26 (FY26) will kickoff the development of sewing threads, both spun and continuous-filament. Phase 0 (COTS evaluation) has already been completed as part of the NESC assessment due to the limited number of FR sewing threads available in the market. The sewing thread project will start with Phase 1 to define requirements, schedule, contract needs, and a testing plan. FY26 also includes initial fiber and fiber blend selection efforts for a next-to-skin knit fabric. Outyears will include further requirements development, setting up contracts, prototyping and testing (Phase 2), and production runs (Phase 3). FY26 objectives: Design of Experiment (DOE) to down select fiber types based on characterization testing (flammability and mechanical) of eleven different knit fabrics swatches Complete first round of prototyping and testing two types of sewing thread (spun and continuous filament)
benefits: An increased use of textiles and other softgoods is crucial to the pursuit of exploration spaceflight to reduce mass and volume. Exploration spaceflight missions benefit from enriched oxygen cabin environments (>30% O2) by allowing a reduced pre-breathe protocol time before EVA. However, materials become exponentially more flammable the higher the O2 levels become. Recent testing within the agency has revealed the lack of commercial-off-the-shelf (COTS) materials that can meet safety requirements in oxygen-enriched environments. Most of the fibers and textiles developed during Apollo (100% O2) and Skylab (70% O2) include various fibers and textiles (i.e., beta glass, PBI, Durette, Astro Velcro) that are no longer commercially available due to those Programs ending and the discontinuation of raw materials or closure of the original manufacturers. More recent vehicle atmospheres like Shuttle and ISS mimic Earth’s atmosphere of 21% O2 and the use of common COTS textiles are acceptable. This project will culminate in various established part numbers and production parameters with vendors so the textiles can be reliably procured in the future for infusion into exploration class missions. Development of new fire-resistant textiles for spaceflight could also benefit industries here on Earth, like Firefighting and emergency response, military and defense, or heavy industry protective equipment.

title: Spacecraft Materials Textiles
lead_organization: Johnson Space Center (JSC) — Houston, Texas
description: The Spacecraft Textile Materials Development for Exploration project focuses on non-flammable IVA textile development and optimization for use in the Exploration Atmosphere (up to 37% O2/8.2 psia), intended for infusion and use in Artemis missions and beyond. A sampling of the textiles needed to outfit a spacecraft cabin include knit and woven fabrics, sewing threads, nonwoven felts/foams including acoustic absorption material, seam sealing tape/fabric, webbing, bungee/elastic cord, and hook and loop fasteners. A variety of textiles will be developed through this project that meet the agency’s most urgent needs. The NASA Engineering and Safety Center (NESC) led an agency-wide technical assessment of NASA's fire-resistant (FR) textile gaps. They released a report with their findings and identified Tier 1 (high-priority) and Tier 2 (lower-priority) textiles based on current agency needs and priorities. The report includes a recommended strategy for closing the FR textile gaps. Each textile development effort will have the same general approach starting with a Commercial-off-the-Shelf (COTS) evaluation (Phase 0) to benchmark the State-of-the-Art (SOA) in a specific textile category. Modified-COTS solutions will be investigated for feasibility to determine if a full development effort is needed. Then there will be planning and baselining (Phase 1) to define requirements, schedule, contract needs, and a testing plan. A contract mechanism will be put in place with a selected vendor for modified-COTS or prototype development (Phase 2). When the prototyping is completed and all requirements are met, a final production run (Phase 3) will be done to establish part numbers and production parameters with the vendor so the textile can be reliably procured in the future for infusion into exploration class missions. Fiscal Year 26 (FY26) will kickoff the development of hook and loop with adhesive backing. Phase 0 (COTS evaluation) has already been completed as part of the NESC assessment due to the limited number of hook and loop vendors in the US. The hook and loop project will start with Phase 1 to define requirements, schedule, contract needs, and a testing plan. FY26 also includes COTS testing of all other Tier 1 textiles to understand the available products and determine which Phase those development projects will begin with. Outyears will include further requirements development, setting up contracts, prototyping and testing (Phase 2), and production runs (Phase 3). FY26 objectives: COTS Testing of Priority Tier 1 textiles identified in the NESC FR Textile Development Strategy Start the customer fire-resistant Hook & Loop with adhesive backing development project – define requirement, vendor selection, and initial prototype trials
benefits: An increased use of textiles and other softgoods is crucial to the pursuit of exploration spaceflight to reduce mass and volume. Exploration spaceflight missions benefit from enriched oxygen cabin environments (>30% O2) by allowing a reduced pre-breathe protocol time before EVA. However, materials become exponentially more flammable the higher the O2 levels become. Recent testing within the agency has revealed the lack of commercial-off-the-shelf (COTS) materials that can meet safety requirements in oxygen-enriched environments. Most of the fibers and textiles developed during Apollo (100% O2) and Skylab (70% O2) include various fibers and textiles (i.e., beta glass, PBI, Durette, Astro Velcro) that are no longer commercially available due to those Programs ending and the discontinuation of raw materials or closure of the original manufacturers. More recent vehicle atmospheres like Shuttle and ISS mimic Earth’s atmosphere of 21% O2 and the use of common COTS textiles are acceptable. This project will culminate in various established part numbers and production parameters with vendors so the textiles can be reliably procured in the future for infusion into exploration class missions. Development of new fire-resistant textiles for spaceflight could also benefit industries here on Earth, like Firefighting and emergency response, military and defense, or heavy industry protective equipment.

title: Forced Air Breathing Mask
lead_organization: Johnson Space Center (JSC) — Houston, Texas
description: NASA has developed a specialized set of emergency response equipment to address fire‑related hazards in spacecraft. Because human spaceflight presents unique operational and safety challenges, much of this equipment has been designed and maintained in‑house as Government Furnished Equipment (GFE). The overall objective is to leverage the 20 plus years of breathing mask experience in the Crew and Thermal Systems Division to identify a new exploration atmosphere ready forced air breathing mask. This effort is important because modern spacecraft often have limited internal volume, and after a fire event, hazardous environments can persist. A breathing mask that does not require a purge would allow crew members to respond more effectively and safely in these conditions. Early activities explore how to leverage the existing Contingency Breathing Apparatus design, including its inhalation port connections, to create commonality between a forced‑air breathing mask and a mask capable of using cartridges for specific hazards such as post‑fire contamination or ammonia exposure. Currently scoped as a feasibility study, this effort aims to demonstrate a proof of concept that could ultimately benefit all space missions. Future efforts will move to complete fabrication of ground prototypes and begin functional and environmental testing to assess performance to requirements.
benefits: Improved crew safety during post‑fire events by providing respiratory protection that does not require crew mask purging. Enhanced emergency response capability for future space missions through quicker, more reliable breathing support. Elimination of the need to switch between different masks after a fire, as a forced‑air mask would meet both purge and post‑fire protection needs.

title: Cold Trap Smoke Eater
lead_organization: Glenn Research Center (GRC) — Cleveland, Ohio
description: A spacecraft fire is particularly hazardous because in addition to the hazardous gaseous and aerosol combustion products that are introduced into the cabin environment, a fire can damage not only the equipment that is the source of the fire but also the systems adjacent to it and poses a serious risk to crew health and safety. Having effective post-fire clean-up equipment and techniques is necessary to remove harmful contaminants and return to a safe cabin atmosphere. A cold trap smoke eater, based on the cold trap filter concept, will be developed under this task to provide a portable emergency response device to quickly remove smoke particles and toxic gases from the environment following a fire in the cabin. It will pull in the smoke-filled air, capture the harmful smoke particles, condense harmful VOCs, and exhaust cool and purified the air back into the cabin. The design of the smoke eater entails various capturing stages and mechanisms to prevent clogging and enhance the collection efficiency and containment of smoke particles. With the addition of sorbent filter stage, it can remove harmful combustion derived gases such as CO and CO2. The smoke eater will be deployed and powered up shortly after the fire has been contained or extinguished and operated until the cabin air has been deemed safe to breath. Most of the capturing stages will be designed and optimized for low air resistance resulting in low power consumption and longer life operation. The final design will be compact and ergonomic to facilitate its use by the crew.
benefits: A cold trap design has the possibility to exceed or complement the performance of other smoke eaters, specifically HEPA-based smoke-eaters which are prone to rapid clogging. Prior testing of a prototype for a Plasma Pyrolysis Assembly (PPA) application producing carbon/soot effluent was demonstrated with > 40% collection efficiency. The proposed design will serve as a pre-filter to capture the bulk mass of smoke particles down to the smallest sizes.

title: Post Fire Cleanup Kit
lead_organization: Glenn Research Center (GRC) — Cleveland, Ohio
description: A spacecraft fire is particularly hazardous due to the inherent danger of fires in closed environments. Having effective post-fire clean-up equipment and techniques is critical as acid gases are very corrosive and stick to surfaces. This could damage hardware or electronics or pose a long-term risk to crew health on exploration duration missions. Post-fire clean-up requires a two-stage approach for clean-up of both the vehicle atmosphere and also clean-up and decontamination of surfaces and potentially damaged equipment. Early project objectives focus on the clean-up and decontamination of surfaces. The goal of FY26 is to complete a market survey and trade study of terrestrial post-fire clean-up processes, with an emphasis on commercial off-the-shelf solutions. The solutions identified through the market survey will then be evaluated for feasibility in application to spaceflight environments and a recommendation for forward work. Solutions may include dry or wet wiping, personal protective equipment, cleaning processes, and containment or disposal of hazardous waste to minimize potential off-gassing.
benefits: This project should identify an ideal product and simple technique that could be used to cleanup fire products from surfaces in a sealed spacecraft environment following a fire emergency during spaceflight.

title: Partial Gravity Portable Fire Suppression System
lead_organization: Glenn Research Center (GRC) — Cleveland, Ohio
description: All NASA space vehicles have had and will have either handheld portable and/or fixed fire suppression systems.
